Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106849; File No. SR-Phlx-2026-70]
November 9, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
1
]
, and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 29, 2026, Nasdaq PHLX LLC (“Phlx” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the Exchange's fees at Equity 7, to establish an optional Nasdaq PSX Monthly Subscription Fee Program (“Program”).
These amendments are effective upon filing. However, they will become operative on November 2, 2026. Therefore, interested firms can sign up for the Program by October 30, 2026, and start operating under the Program in the trading month that begins on November 2, 2026.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​phlx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend the Exchange's fee schedule at Equity 7, by establishing an optional Nasdaq PSX Monthly Subscription Fee Program. The rule text for the Program will be located in Section 3 of Equity 7.
The Exchange is proposing to establish the Program as a completely voluntary and optional monthly alternative to its regular fee schedule, which charges firms
[
3
]
separate fees for each product or service they consume, including per share executed fees for removing liquidity on the Exchange during the month. Although the existing fee schedule is competitive and works well for many firms, the Exchange observes that for some firms, the existing fee schedule fails to incentivize increased participation on the Exchange. To address this concern, and to make participation in the Exchange more predictable and ultimately more attractive, the Exchange proposes to offer its firms the option to pay a single subscription fee each month.
Under the Program, a firm would be charged a flat fee of $650,000 a month. This fee will include an allocation of up to five order entry ports (
i.e.
OUCH, FIX, RASH) on Nasdaq PSX. It will also include liquidity-removing executions on Nasdaq PSX during the month—up to and including 0.125% of Consolidated Volume
[
4
]
in the prior
(
printed page 73325)
month (rounded up to the nearest whole share).
[
5
]
Any liquidity-removing executions during the month on Nasdaq PSX that exceed 0.125% of Consolidated Volume in the prior month (rounded up to the nearest whole share) will be charged a fee of $0.0027 per share. Participation in the Program will not affect a firm's ability to earn rebates for providing liquidity on the Exchange.
The Program would be entirely voluntary and optional. Any firm that does not sign up for the Program will be charged the default rates under Section 3 of Equity 7. To sign up for the Program, a firm must notify the Exchange before noon (Eastern Time) on the last trading day of the prior month.
[
6
]
Likewise, a firm may withdraw from the Program by notifying the Exchange before noon (Eastern Time) on the last trading day of the prior month.
[
7
]
A firm will remain enrolled in the Program unless it notifies the Exchange of its withdrawal from the same.
The Exchange designed this fee to reflect the existing liquidity-removing execution and order entry protocol use of its firms, while also providing a cost-effective pathway for them to grow their participation on Nasdaq PSX. For firms whose current and expected activity aligns with this subscription fee model, the program could offer meaningful monthly savings compared with the existing regular fee schedule as their activity on Nasdaq PSX continues to grow. That said, each firm should evaluate for itself its expected needs and activities to determine whether the subscription fee or the regular fee schedule is appropriate.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
8
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
9
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange's proposed changes to its fee schedule are reasonable in several respects. As a threshold matter, the Exchange is subject to significant competitive forces in the market for equity securities transaction services that constrain its pricing determinations in that market. The fact that this market is competitive has long been recognized by the courts. In
NetCoalition
v.
Securities and Exchange Commission,
the D.C. Circuit stated as follows: “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce .' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .”
[
10
]
The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
11
]
Numerous indicia demonstrate the competitive nature of this market. For example, clear substitutes to the Exchange exist in the market for equity security transaction services. The Exchange is only one of several equity venues to which market participants may direct their order flow. Competing equity exchanges offer similar tiered pricing structures to that of the Exchange, including schedules of rebates and fees that apply based upon members achieving certain volume thresholds.
Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules. As such, the proposal represents a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase its liquidity and market share relative to its competitors.
The Exchange believes that the proposed Program is reasonable because it would provide firms with an additional, simple, and predictable monthly pricing alternative for their Nasdaq PSX order entry protocol use and liquidity-removing execution activity, while retaining the flexibility to choose to continue being subject to regular transactions fees and port fees. A firm that elects the Program would pay a monthly fee that includes up to five order entry ports and liquidity-removing executions on Nasdaq PSX during the month up to and including 0.125% of Consolidated Volume in the prior month, while liquidity-removing executions above that level would be subject to the stated per-share fee. Firms that do not believe the Program is appropriate for their business, trading strategy, or expected liquidity-removing volume may choose not to enroll and instead remain subject to the default rates in Section 3 of Equity 7. The proposal therefore adds pricing choice rather than replacing the existing fee schedule.
The Exchange believes that the Program is reasonable, as it is a voluntary alternative to its regular fee schedule, which charges firms separate fees for each product or service they consume, including per share executed fees for removing liquidity on the Exchange during the month. Although the existing fee schedule is competitive and works well for many firms, the Exchange observes that for some firms, the existing fee schedule is complex and onerous to navigate, and that it fails to incentivize increased participation on the Exchange. To address this concern, which the Commission itself has expressed in the past, and to make participation in the Exchange easier, simpler, more predictable and ultimately more attractive, the Exchange believes that it is reasonable and consistent with the Act to offer its firms the option to pay a single subscription
(
printed page 73326)
fee each month. The monthly fee would encompass a single flat monthly subscription fee to cover many if not most of their trading activities on the Exchange.
The Exchange also believes that the proposed Program is an equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges. The Program would be available to all firms on the same terms, and the monthly fee would apply only to firms that affirmatively choose to receive the bundled package of order entry ports and liquidity-removing executions covered by the Program. The included liquidity-removing execution volume threshold is based on current month activity of firms and prior-month Consolidated Volume, an objective and transparent measure already used in Equity 7 to determine transaction pricing, and the use of these appropriate measurement periods provides firms with greater certainty when deciding whether to elect the Program for a particular month. The Exchange believes that it is equitable to offer a monthly alternative that may be attractive to firms whose expected usage would make the Program efficient, while preserving the existing default pricing structure for firms that do not elect the Program.
The Exchange further believes that the proposed Program is not unfairly discriminatory. The Program would be offered to all firms in a uniform manner, and any differences in the economic effect of the Program would result from a firm's voluntary decision to enroll and its own level of Nasdaq PSX usage. Firms that determine that the Program would not be beneficial may continue to access Nasdaq PSX under the Exchange's otherwise-applicable pricing schedule. As a result, the proposal does not favor or penalize any particular firm, but instead permits each firm to choose the pricing option that best aligns with its business needs.
Finally, the Exchange believes that the Program is consistent with the Act because it may encourage additional order flow to Nasdaq PSX and thereby enhance market quality. By providing a firm with greater cost certainty for a specified amount of order entry and liquidity-removing execution activity, the Program may incentivize firms to direct additional orders to Nasdaq PSX. Additional order flow and liquidity on Nasdaq PSX may benefit all market participants by increasing liquidity-removing execution opportunities and contributing to a more robust market. If the Program does not provide sufficient value to firms, they may decline to enroll or withdraw from the Program, and they remain free to route order flow to other venues.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. In terms of inter-market competition, the Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive, or rebate opportunities available at other venues to be more favorable. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and with alternative trading systems that have been exempted from compliance with the statutory standards applicable to exchanges. Because competitors are free to modify their own fees in response, and because market participants may readily adjust their order routing practices, the Exchange believes that the degree to which fee changes in this market may impose any burden on competition is extremely limited.
The Exchange does not believe that the Program will impose any burden on intra-market competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Program would be voluntary, and it would be available to all firms on the same terms. No firm would be required to enroll in the Program, and a firm that does not enroll would continue to be charged the default rates under Section 3 of Equity 7. Likewise, a firm that enrolls but later determines that the Program is no longer attractive may withdraw by providing timely notice to the Exchange. The Program therefore would not place any category of firm at a competitive disadvantage; rather, it would add an optional pricing alternative that each firm may evaluate based on its own expected Nasdaq PSX usage.
The Exchange also does not believe that the Program will impose any burden on inter-market competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. Nasdaq PSX operates in a highly competitive market in which firms can readily direct order flow to competing equities exchanges or off-exchange venues if they view the Exchange's pricing as unattractive. The Program does not restrict the ability of any competing venue to modify its own fees, credits, connectivity charges, or pricing programs in response. To the extent the Program succeeds, it will do so because firms voluntarily determine that the Program provides value relative to available alternatives.
For these reasons, the Exchange believes that the Program may promote competition by giving firms an additional way to access Nasdaq PSX and manage their anticipated transaction and order entry costs. The proposal does not eliminate any existing pricing option, does not require firms to purchase any new service, and does not prevent other venues from offering similar or different pricing alternatives. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that any competitive effect of the proposal would be limited and consistent with the Exchange's need to compete for order flow in the national market system.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
12
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106848; File No. SR-NYSEAMER-2026-98]
November 9, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that, on October 28, 2026, NYSE American LLC (“NYSE American” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the Connectivity Fee Schedule regarding colocation services and fees to update the list of included data products. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
(
printed page 73332)
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend the Connectivity Fee Schedule regarding colocation services and fees to update the list of included data products (“Included Data Products”).
Currently, the table of Included Data Products in Colocation Note 4 sets forth the market data feeds that Users
[
4
]
can connect to at no additional cost when they purchase a service that includes access to the LCN or IP network.
[
5
]
The Exchange proposes to update the table of Included Data Products to include NYSE Options Select, a data feed that consists of a subset of data from the OPRA consolidated data feed that has been curated by the Exchange's Affiliate SRO NYSE.
[
6
]
Given the growing number of options series and the increasing popularity of options trading, the OPRA consolidated data feed is voluminous and requires market participants to dedicate significant amounts of bandwidth to receive it. The NYSE Options Select data feed would provide market participants the ability to view critical NBBO, trade data, and administrative messages from the OPRA data feed without consuming the full OPRA data set, thereby decreasing bandwidth requirements and costs when compared to the full OPRA data feed. Other exchange groups currently offer similar selections of the OPRA data feed, including the Nasdaq Smart Options
[
7
]
and Cboe Options Lite
[
8
]
data feeds.
To implement the change, the Exchange proposes to update the table of Included Data Products as follows (proposed addition italicized):
NYSE Bonds.
NYSE Options Select.
NYSE Options Select Trades & NBBO.
NYSE Options Select Trades & NBBO Snapshot.
NYSE Texas.
NYSE Texas Aggregated Lite.
NYSE Texas BBO.
NYSE Texas Integrated Feed.
NYSE Texas Order Imbalances.
NYSE Texas Trades.
As indicated, the Exchange plans to offer connectivity to two different NYSE Options Select data feeds: NYSE Options Select Trades & NBBO, which includes real-time trades and real-time NBBO updates for all OPRA symbols, and NYSE Options Select Trades & NBBO Snapshot, which includes real-time trades for all OPRA symbols plus an NBBO snapshot at the time of a trade (collectively the “NYSE Options Select data feeds”).
The Exchange does not charge for connectivity to the Included Data Feeds. Accordingly, it would not charge for connectivity to the NYSE Options Select data feeds.
Application and Impact of the Proposed Changes
The proposed rule change would not apply differently to distinct types or sizes of market participants. Rather, it would apply to all Users equally. As is currently the case, the purchase of any colocation service is completely voluntary and the Connectivity Fee Schedule is applied uniformly to all Users.
The proposed change is not otherwise intended to address any other issues relating to colocation services or related fees, and the Exchange is not aware of any problems that Users would have in complying with the proposed change.
Implementation
The proposed rule change will become operational when the NYSE Options Select data feeds are available. The Exchange will announce the date through a customer notice.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
10
]
in particular, because it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest and because it is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers. The Exchange further believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
11
]
because it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members and issuers and other persons using its facilities.
The Proposed Rule Change Is Reasonable
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is reasonable and would perfect the mechanisms of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest, because adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds would increase the number of Included Data Products available to Users for no additional charge. All Users that voluntarily select to access the LCN or IP network would not be subject to a charge above and beyond the fee paid for the relevant LCN or IP network access. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposed change is reasonable because the change would mean that a User would have the option of adding connectivity to additional market data feeds without paying additional charges.
Adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds to the list of Included Data Products would allow a User to connect to the NYSE Options Select data feeds if it wished but would not require it to do so. As currently, a User would be able to determine which Included Data Products, if any, to which it connects,
(
printed page 73333)
based on what would best serve its needs, tailoring the service to the requirements of its business operations.
By adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds, the proposed change would ensure that the list of Included Data Products was up to date. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is reasonable and would perfect the mechanisms of a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, protect investors and the public interest, as it would ensure that the description of Included Data Products was complete, ensuring that it is accessible and transparent, and providing market participants with clarity as to what connectivity is included in the purchase of access to the LCN and IP networks.
The Proposed Rule Change Is Equitable and Not Unfairly Discriminatory
The Exchange believes that the proposed change provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members and issuers and other persons using its facilities and does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers because adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds would increase the number of Included Data Products available to Users for no additional charge. All Users that voluntarily select to access the LCN or IP network would not be subject to a charge above and beyond the fee paid for the relevant LCN or IP network access. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposed change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because the change would mean that a User would have the option of adding connectivity to an additional market data feed without paying additional charges.
Further, the Exchange believes that the proposed change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory since, as is true now, the proposed change would not apply differently to distinct types or sizes of Users but would apply to all Users equally. Moreover, adding the proposed additional Included Data Products would allow a User to connect to the NYSE Options Select data feeds if it wished, but would not require it to do so. As now, a User would be able to determine which Included Data Products, if any, to which it connects, based on what would best serve its needs, tailoring the service to the requirements of its business operations.
By adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds, the proposed change would ensure that the list of Included Data Products was up to date. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory, as it would ensure that the description of Included Data Products was complete, ensuring that it is accessible and transparent, and providing market participants with clarity as to what connectivity is included in the purchase of access to the LCN and IP networks.
For the reasons above, the proposed changes do not unfairly discriminate between or among market participants that are otherwise capable of satisfying any applicable co-location fees, requirements, terms, and conditions established from time to time by the Exchange.
For these reasons, the Exchange believes that the proposal is consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange believes that the proposal will not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of Section 6(b)(8) of the Act.
[
12
]
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act because adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds would increase the number of Included Data Products available to Users for no additional charge. All Users that voluntarily select to access the LCN or IP network would not be subject to a charge above and beyond the fee paid for the relevant LCN or IP network access. Accordingly, the change would mean that a User would have the option of adding connectivity to an additional market data feed without paying additional charges.
Adding the proposed additional Included Data Product would allow a User to connect to the NYSE Options Select data feeds if it wished, but would not require it to do so. In this way, the proposed changes would enhance competition by, as now, enabling a User to determine to which Included Data Products, if any, it connects, based on what would best serve its needs, tailoring the service to the requirements of its business operations.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act because, as with the other Included Data Products, it believes it would not be the exclusive method to connect to the NYSE Options Select data feeds. As alternatives to connecting to the NYSE Options Select data feeds as an Included Data Products, a User may connect to the market data feed through another User or through a connection to an Exchange access center outside the data center, third party access center, or third party vendor. In addition, a User may choose instead to connect to a similar product offered by another exchange, such as Nasdaq Smart Options or Cboe Options Lite.
[
13
]
By adding the NYSE Options Select data feeds, the proposed change would ensure that the list of Included Data Products was up to date. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the proposed addition to the description of Included Data Products would make the description more accessible and transparent. In this manner, the proposed change would provide market participants with clarity as to what connectivity is included in the purchase of access to the LCN and IP networks, thereby enhancing competition by ensuring that all Users have access to the same information regarding the Included Data Products.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
14
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
15
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
[
16
]
(
printed page 73334)
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
17
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
18
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposal may become operative immediately upon filing. The Exchange believes that waiver of the 30-day operative delay would allow the Exchange to promptly provide market participants with another choice for obtaining streamlined options data as the Exchange anticipates that the NYSE Options Select data feeds will be ready for launch in fewer than 30 days. The Commission believes that waiver of the operative delay would be consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest because the proposed rule change does not present any novel issues and it would provide investors with an additional option for accessing potentially helpful information that could inform their trading decisions as soon as the feeds are available. Accordingly, the Commission hereby waives the 30-day operative delay and designates the proposed rule change operative upon filing.
[
19
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-98 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-98. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-98 and should be submitted on or before December 4, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
20
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

full_text:

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106847; File No. SR-PHLX-2026-69]
November 9, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 29, 2026, Nasdaq PHLX LLC (“PHLX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to increase the PHLX Options Regulatory Fee (“ORF”) rate that will be effective on November 1, 2026. Additionally, the Exchange proposes a non-substantive change to Options 7, Section 6(D), to delete obsolete rule text that described a prior ORF collection methodology.
While the changes proposed herein are effective upon filing, the Exchange has designated the proposed rule change to be operative on November 1, 2026.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​phlx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
At this time, PHLX proposes to increase the ORF rate from $0.0080 to $0.0090 per contract side, effective November 1, 2026. This rate change is influenced by a review of regulatory costs and realized options volumes at the Exchange. Additionally, the Exchange proposes a non-substantive change to Options 7, Section 6(D), to delete obsolete rule text that described a prior ORF collection methodology.
PHLX assesses ORF for options transactions cleared by The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”) in the customer
[
3
]
range, however ORF is assessed to each PHLX member organization
[
4
]
for executions that occur on PHLX. Specifically, the ORF is collected by OCC on behalf of PHLX from member organizations and non-member organizations for all customer transactions executed on PHLX. ORF is assessed and collected on ultimately cleared customer contracts, taking into account adjustments for CMTA that were provided to PHLX the same day as the trade.
[
5
]
Further, the Exchange bills ORF according to the clearing instructions provided on the execution. More specifically, PHLX assesses ORF based on the clearing instruction provided on the execution on trade date and does not take into consideration CMTA changes or transfers that occur at OCC.
[
6
]
PHLX ensures that ORF Regulatory Revenue
[
7
]
does not exceed a material portion of Options Regulatory Costs.
[
8
]
More specifically, PHLX endeavors to ensure that ORF Regulatory Revenue generated from ORF does not exceed 82% of Options Regulatory Costs. The Exchange will notify member organizations via an Options Trader Alert of any change in the amount of the
(
printed page 73338)
fee at least 30 calendar days prior to the effective date of the change.
[
9
]
As is the case today, PHLX will monitor ORF Regulatory Revenue to ensure that it, in combination with other regulatory fees and fines, does not exceed Options Regulatory Costs. In determining whether an expense is considered an Options Regulatory Costs, the Exchange will continue to review all costs and make determinations whether there is a nexus between the expense and a regulatory function. The Exchange notes that fines collected by the Exchange in connection with a disciplinary matter will continue to offset Options Regulatory Costs.
ORF Regulatory Revenue is designed to recover a material portion of the Options Regulatory Costs to the Exchange for the supervision and regulation of member organizations' transactions, including performing routine surveillances, investigations, examinations, financial monitoring, and policy, rulemaking, interpretive, and enforcement activities. Options Regulatory Costs include direct regulatory expenses
[
10
]
and certain indirect expenses in support of the regulatory function.
[
11
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
12
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
13
]
which provides that Exchange rules may provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members, and other persons using its facilities. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
14
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes the proposed increase of the ORF rate is reasonable because of lower-than-expected options volumes at the Exchange have resulted in lower-than-expected ORF Regulatory Revenue. Increasing the ORF rate would increase the ORF Regulatory Revenue, while continuing to ensure that ORF Regulatory Revenue does not exceed a material portion of the Exchange's Options Regulatory Costs. As noted above, the ORF is designed to recover a material portion, but not all, of the Exchange's Options Regulatory Costs.
The Exchange designed the ORF to generate ORF Regulatory Revenue that would be less than the Exchange's Options Regulatory Costs, thereby ensuring that such revenue, in combination with other regulatory fees and fines, does not exceed Options Regulatory Costs. This is consistent with the view of the Commission that regulatory fees be used for regulatory purposes and not to support the Exchange's business operations. As discussed above; however, after review of its Options Regulatory Costs and ORF Regulatory Revenue, which includes revenues from ORF and other regulatory fees and fines, the Exchange determined that absent an increase in the ORF rate it may collect ORF Regulatory Revenue that would fall significantly short of its Options Regulatory Costs. Indeed, the Exchange notes that when taking into account options volume, it estimates that the current ORF rate, if left unchanged, may generate ORF Regulatory Revenue that would fall short of the targeted 82% of the Exchange's projected Options Regulatory Costs. As such, the Exchange believes it is reasonable and appropriate to increase the ORF rate from $0.0080 to $0.0090 per contract side.
The Exchange also believes the proposed fee change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because collecting 82% of Options Regulatory Costs is appropriate and correlates to the degree of regulatory responsibility and Options Regulatory Costs borne by the Exchange with respect to customer transactions. The Exchange's proposal continues to ensure that Options Regulatory Revenue, in combination with other regulatory fees and fines, does not exceed Options Regulatory Costs. Fines collected by the Exchange in connection with a disciplinary matter will continue to offset Options Regulatory Costs. Continuing to cap ORF collected at 82% of Options Regulatory Costs is reasonable, equitable and not unfairly discriminatory as the Options Regulatory Revenue collected will offset the corresponding Options Regulatory Costs associated with on exchange customer transactions. The Exchange will review the ORF Regulatory Revenue and will amend the ORF if it finds that its ORF Regulatory Revenue exceeds its projections.
Finally, deleting obsolete rule text at Options 7, Section 6(D), is a non-substantive change that is designed to keep the Exchange rule book current, and thus make it easier to understand.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition

Furthermore, the Exchange will continue to review its ORF Regulatory Revenue and would amend the ORF if it finds that its ORF Regulatory Revenue exceeds its projections.
The proposed change to the ORF rate does not impose an undue burden on inter-market competition because ORF is a regulatory fee that supports regulation in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange notes, however, the proposed change is not designed to address any competitive issues. The Exchange is obligated to ensure that the amount of ORF Regulatory Revenue, in combination with its other regulatory fees and fines, does not exceed Options Regulatory Cost.
Finally, deleting obsolete rule text at Options 7, Section 6(D), is a non-substantive change and, therefore, has no impact on competition.

1. Purpose

[
3
]
range, however ORF is assessed to each MRX Member
[
4

for executions that occur on MRX. Specifically, the ORF is collected by OCC on behalf of MRX from Members and non-members for all customer transactions executed on MRX. [
5

6

MRX ensures that ORF Regulatory Revenue
[
7
]
does not exceed a material portion of Options Regulatory Costs.
[
8
]
More specifically, MRX endeavors to ensure that ORF Regulatory Revenue generated from ORF does not exceed 82% of Options Regulatory Costs. [
9
]
As is the case today, MRX will monitor ORF Regulatory Revenue to ensure that it, in combination with other regulatory fees and fines, does not exceed Options Regulatory Costs. The Exchange notes that fines collected by the Exchange in connection with a disciplinary matter will continue to offset Options Regulatory Costs.

10
]
and certain indirect expenses in support of the regulatory function.
[
11
]

12
]

13
]

[
14
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.

Fines collected by the Exchange in connection with a disciplinary matter will continue to offset Options
(
printed page 73331)
Regulatory Costs. Finally, deleting obsolete rule text at Options 7, Section 5(C), is a non-substantive change and, therefore, has no impact on competition.

title: Horse Protection

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
On May 8, 2024, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the United States Department of Agriculture published in the
Federal Register
a final rule that amended the regulations promulgated under the Horse Protection Act (the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule). APHIS is proposing to remove the provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule that have been vacated by court order and proposing to withdraw the remaining non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule to ensure that the regulations afford due process and better align with the Act. APHIS is also proposing to amend the regulations by revising, among other things, the certification requirements for training and licensing of designated qualified persons (DQPs); enhancing DQP inspection procedures and the process for appealing APHIS inspections before any possible disqualification by management; and clarifying that if a horse is determined to be sore, it is disqualified from participating in the class in which the inspection took place and not the entire event.
DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov
.
Enter APHIS-2026-0067 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.

Send your comment to Docket No.  APHIS-2026-0067, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Ave, Beltsville, MD, 20740.
Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
Regulations.gov
or in our reading room, which is located in room 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dr. Martha Keller, DVM, Director of the Center for Animal Welfare, Animal Care, 2150 Centre Ave. Bldg. B, Mailstop 3W11, Fort Collins, CO 80526; (970) 821-5734.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Under the Horse Protection Act (HPA, or the Act,
15 U.S.C. 1821
et seq.
), the Secretary of Agriculture is authorized to promulgate regulations necessary to carry out the purposes of the Act, which include eliminating the cruel practice of soring horses and promoting fair competition.
The Secretary has delegated responsibility for administering the Act to the Administrator of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA's) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). Within APHIS, the responsibility for administering the Act has been delegated to the Deputy Administrator for Animal Care. Regulations established under the Act are contained in
9 CFR part 11
(referred to below as the regulations), and
9 CFR part 12
lists the rules of practice governing administrative proceedings.
In the three headings immediately below, we provide a summary, first, of the sections of the Act, then, of the sections of the current regulations, and lastly, of the sections of the final rule we published on May 8, 2024, referred to below as the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule (
89 FR 39194-39251
, Docket No. APHIS-2022-0004).
Summary of the Horse Protection Act
The current structure of the HPA is summarized below.
Section 1821 of the Act, “Definitions” (
15 U.S.C. 1821
), contains definitions of terms used in the Act. Saliently for this proposed rule, the Act defines a “sore” horse as follows: “The term `sore' when used to describe a horse means that:
(A) an irritating or blistering agent has been applied, internally or externally, by a person to any limb of a horse,
(B) any burn, cut, or laceration has been inflicted by a person on any limb of a horse,
(C) any tack, nail, screw, or chemical agent has been injected by a person into or used by a person on any limb of a horse, or
(D) any other substance or device has been used by a person on any limb of a horse or a person has engaged in a practice involving a horse, and, as a result of such application, infliction, injection, use, or practice, such horse suffers, or can reasonably be expected to suffer, physical pain or distress, inflammation, or lameness when walking, trotting, or otherwise moving, except that such term does not include such an application, infliction, injection, use, or practice in connection with the therapeutic treatment of a horse by or under the supervision of a person licensed to practice veterinary medicine in the State in which such treatment was given.”
Section 1822 of the Act contains a Congressional statement of findings. In addition to declaring that the soring of horses is cruel and inhumane, Congress further finds that the movement, showing, exhibition, or sale of sore horses in intrastate commerce adversely affects and burdens interstate and foreign commerce and creates unfair competition.
Section 1823 of the Act contains requirements pertaining to horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions. Paragraph (a) of the section requires the management of horse shows and exhibitions to disqualify any horse from being shown or exhibited if the horse is sore or if the management has been notified by a person appointed by the management in accordance with regulations issued by USDA or by USDA that the horse is sore.
Paragraph (b) of the section contains similar requirements directed to the management of horse sales or auctions and prohibits sore horses from being sold, auctioned, or exhibited for the purpose of sale.
Paragraph (c) of the section requires the Secretary to prescribe, by regulation, requirements for the appointment by the management (of any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction) of persons qualified to detect and diagnose a horse which is sore or to otherwise inspect horses for the purposes of enforcing the Act (referred to as a designated qualified person, or DQP, below). The paragraph further prohibits the appointment of persons who, after notice and opportunity for a hearing, have been disqualified by the Secretary to make such detection, diagnosis, or inspection and prohibits any person appointed by management from conducting inspections in a manner other than that set forth in paragraph (e) of the same section, which contains conditions for USDA's inspection of horses.
Paragraph (d) of the section requires the management of horse shows, horse exhibitions, horse sales, and auctions to maintain records, make reports, and
(
printed page 73381)
provide information, as the Secretary may by regulation reasonably require for the purposes of implementing or to determine compliance with the Act. It also requires management to permit entry of officers and employees duly designated by the Secretary, upon request and at all reasonable times, in order for the officers or employees to inspect or copy such records.
Finally, paragraph (e) of the section provides that the Secretary or any representative of the Secretary duly designated by the Secretary, may inspect any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction or any horse at such events for purposes of enforcing the HPA.
Section 1824 lists prohibited acts under the Act. The following acts are prohibited:
Shipping, transporting, moving, delivering, or receiving a horse which is sore and with reason to believe that such horse while it is sore may be shown, exhibited, entered for the purposes of being shown or exhibited, sold, auctioned, or offered for sale in any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, with exceptions for common or contract carriers and their employees;
Showing or exhibiting at a horse show or exhibition any horse which is sore; entering any horse which is sore at a horse show or exhibition for the purpose of showing or exhibiting the horse; selling, auctioning, or offering for sale, in any horse show or auction, any horse which is sore; or allowing the owner of a sore horse to engage in any of the above activities;
If management of a horse show or exhibition does not appoint and retain a designated qualified person, failing to disqualify a horse which is sore from being shown or exhibited;
If management of a horse sale or auction does not appoint and retain a designated qualified person, failing to prohibit the sale, offering for sale, or auction of a horse which is sore;
If management of a horse show or exhibition appoints and retains a designated qualified person, failing to disqualify a horse which is sore from being shown or exhibited, when management has knowledge that the horse is sore or after the management has been informed by the inspector or USDA that the horse is sore;
Showing or exhibiting, selling or auctioning; allowing to be shown, exhibited, or sold; entering for purposes of showing or exhibiting; or offering for sale a horse that “is wearing or bearing any equipment, device, paraphernalia, or substance” that the Secretary by regulation prohibits to prevent the soring of horses;
Failing to establish, maintain, or submit records, notices, reports, or other information as required by the Act and regulations established under the Act;
Failing or refusing to permit access to or copying of records, or failing or refusing to permit entry or inspection as required by the Act;
Removing any marking required by the Secretary to identify a horse as being detained; and
Failing or refusing to provide USDA with adequate space or facilities, as prescribed by regulation, in which to conduct inspections or other authorized activities.
Section 1825 of the Act allows for the assessment of criminal and civil penalties for violations of the Act; provides for judicial review of civil penalties; allows USDA to disqualify from showing or exhibiting any horse, judging or managing any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction persons who have been convicted in a criminal case for violating the Act, who have paid a civil penalty assessed under the Act, or who are subject to a final order assessing a civil penalty under the Act; and sets forth procedures for such a hearing. The section also allows USDA to detain for up to 24 hours a horse which is sore, or which USDA has probable cause to believe is sore, at a horse show, exhibition, or horse sale, or auction, for purposes of examination, testing, or taking of evidence; and to temporarily mark any detained horse. It also prohibits detained horses from being moved without authorization from the place they are detained. It also establishes a presumption that a horse is sore if it manifests abnormal sensitivity or inflammation in both of its forelimbs or both of its hindlimbs in any civil or criminal action to enforce the Act or regulations.
Section 1826 requires the Secretary to notify the Attorney General if the Secretary believes a willful violation of the Act has occurred and prosecution is needed to obtain compliance, while also allowing the Attorney General to take such action as deemed necessary.
Section 1827 directs the USDA to use, to the maximum extent practicable, existing USDA personnel and facilities in carrying out the purposes of the Act. With the consent of a State, USDA may also use State officers and employees to assist in carrying out the Act. USDA is also authorized to provide technical and other nonfinancial assistance to a State to assist it in enforcing State laws that prohibit conduct that is also prohibited in the Act.
Section 1828 allows USDA to issue rules and regulations necessary to carry out the Act; section 1829 contains terms related to Federal preemption and concurrent jurisdiction; and section 1831 authorizes appropriations to carry out the Act. (Section 1830 is omitted).
Summary of Current Regulations
The current structure of the regulations in
9 CFR parts 11
and
12
is summarized below.
Section 11.1, “Definitions,” lists the definitions for terms used throughout part 11. It contains definitions of the following terms:
Act, Action device, Administrator, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), APHIS representative, APHIS Show Veterinarian, Department, Designated Qualified Person
or
DQP, Exhibitor, Horse, Horse exhibition, Horse industry organization or association, Horse sale or horse auction, Horse show, Inspection, Lubricant, Management, Person, Regional Director, Secretary, Show manager, Sore,
Sponsoring organization,
and
State.
Section 11.2, “Prohibitions concerning exhibitors,” lists general and specific prohibitions for any device, method, practice, or substance used on any horse at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, competition restrictions for 2-year-old Tennessee Walking Horses (TWHs) and racking horses; and horse-related information requirements under the Act and regulations.
In § 11.2(a), the general prohibitions state that, “Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph (b) of this section, no chain, boot, roller, collar, action device, nor any other device, method, practice, or substance shall be used with respect to any horse at any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction if such use causes or can reasonably be expected to cause such horse to be sore.” Specific prohibitions regarding devices, equipment, or practices on any horse at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction are listed in paragraph (b) of § 11.2.
Paragraph (c) prohibits all substances on the extremities above the hoof of any TWH or racking horse while being shown, exhibited, or offered for sale at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, except lubricants such as glycerin, petrolatum, and mineral oil, or mixtures thereof, which are furnished by the horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction. Lubricants can only be applied after the horse has been inspected by management or by a designated qualified person, and lubricants that will be applied must be made available to APHIS personnel for inspection and sampling as deemed necessary.
Paragraph (d) provides specific requirements for rest periods during horse show and horse exhibition
(
printed page 73382)
workouts or performances for 2-year-old TWHs and racking horses and working exhibitions for 2-year-old TWHs and racking horses at sales or auctions.
Paragraph (e) prohibits failing to provide information or providing any false or misleading information required by the Act or regulations or requested by Department representatives, by any person that owns, trains, shows, exhibits, or sells or has custody of, or direction or control over any horse shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned or entered for the purpose of being shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned at any horse show, exhibition, or horse sale or auction.
Under § 11.3, “Scar rule,” horses that do not meet the scar rule criteria are considered sore and are subject to all prohibitions of the Act. Paragraph (a) of § 11.3 states that the “anterior and anterior-lateral surfaces of the fore pasterns (extensor surface)” are required to “be free of bilateral granulomas, other bilateral pathological evidence of inflammation, and, other bilateral evidence of abuse indicative of soring including, but not limited to, excessive loss of hair.” This section includes a footnote defining a granuloma as “any one of a rather large group of fairly distinctive focal lesions that are formed as a result of inflammatory reactions caused by biological, chemical, or physical agents.”
Paragraph (b) of § 11.3 states that the “posterior surfaces of the pasterns (flexor surface), including the sulcus or `pocket' may show bilateral areas of uniformly thickened epithelial tissue if such areas are free of proliferating granuloma tissue, irritation, moisture, edema, or other evidence of inflammation.”
Section 11.4, “Inspection and detention of horses,” includes requirements regarding inspection of horses by APHIS representatives, as well as detention of horses for inspection if an APHIS representative has probable cause to believe that a horse is sore. This section also includes provisions for maintaining the well-being of a horse in detention and for informing the owner, trainer, exhibitor, or other person having immediate custody of or responsibility for any horse allegedly found to be in violation of the Act or the regulations, of such alleged violation before the horse is released from detention. Provisions for requesting reexamination and testing of detained horses within a 24-hour period are also included in this section.
Under § 11.5, “Access to premises and records,” paragraph (a) provides that the management “shall, without fee, charge, assessment, or other compensation, provide APHIS representatives with unlimited access to the grandstands, sale ring, barns, stables, grounds, offices, and all other areas of any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction, including any adjacent areas under their direction, control, or supervision for the purpose of inspecting any horses, or any records required to be kept by regulation or otherwise maintained.” Management must also provide “an adequate, safe, and accessible area for the visual inspection and observation of horses while such horses are competitively or otherwise performing at any horse show or horse exhibition, or while such horses are being sold or auctioned or offered for sale or auction at any horse sale or horse auction.”
Paragraph (b) of § 11.5 states that, “Each horse owner, exhibitor, or other person having custody of or responsibility for any horse at any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction shall, without fee, charge, assessment, or other compensation, admit any APHIS representative or Designated Qualified Person appointed by management, to all areas of barns, compounds, horse vans, horse trailers, stables, stalls, paddocks, or other show, exhibition, or sale or auction grounds or related areas at any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction, for the purpose of inspecting any such horse at any and all reasonable times.” Such persons must also promptly present their horses for inspection upon notification, orally or in writing, by any APHIS representative or DQP appointed by management for the purpose of determining whether such horse is in compliance with the Act and regulations.
Section 11.6, “Inspection space and facility requirements,” requires the management of every horse show, exhibition, or horse sale or auction containing TWHs or racking horses to provide, without fee, sufficient space and facilities for APHIS representatives to carry out their duties under the Act and regulations, whether or not management has received prior notification by APHIS. The management of every horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction which does not contain TWHs or racking horses must provide, without fee, sufficient space and facilities when requested to do so by APHIS representatives. Space and facility requirements include sufficient space, in a convenient location, for inspecting horses; protection from the elements; a means to control crowds and onlookers; an accessible, reliable, and convenient 110-volt electrical power source, if electrical service is available at the site and is requested by the APHIS representative; and appropriate inspection waiting and detention areas.
Section 11.7, “Certification and licensing of designated qualified persons (DQP's),” sets forth the qualifications and requirements for DQPs and DQP programs. Paragraph (a) of § 11.7, “Basic qualifications of DQP applicants,” lists basic professional qualifications required of DQP applicants and paragraph (b) lists certification requirements for DQP programs initiated and maintained by horse industry organizations or associations (HIOs). As part of maintaining a certified DQP program, HIOs are responsible for selecting, training, and licensing DQPs.
Paragraph (c) of § 11.7 contains DQP licensing requirements and paragraph (d) lists recordkeeping and other requirements to be met by HIOs and DQPs. Paragraph (d) provides that HIOs must submit records on a monthly basis to APHIS containing details of horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions at which DQPs appointed by management inspect horses. Paragraph (e) of § 11.7 prohibits the management of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction from appointing any person to detect and diagnose horses which are sore or to otherwise inspect horses for the purpose of enforcing the Act if such person does not hold a valid DQP license, if the license is canceled, or if, after notice and opportunity for a hearing, the person has been disqualified by the Secretary from performing diagnosis, detection, and inspection under the Act.
Paragraph (f) contains provisions for canceling a DQP license. Concluding this section, paragraph (g) provides the process for revoking the DQP program certification of an HIO after notice and opportunity for a hearing.
Sections 11.8 through 11.18 currently are omitted from Part 11.
Section 11.19 provides for the authorization and inspection of Horse Protection Inspectors (HPIs). This section was added to the regulations in May 2024 Horse Protection final rule to replace DQPs with HPIs. For reasons discussed below, it is the only section of the final rule in effect.
Paragraph (a) of § 11.20 lists the responsibilities and liabilities of the management of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction which does not appoint and retain a DQP to inspect horses, noting that in such cases, management is responsible for identifying all horses that are sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations and disqualifying or disallowing any such horses from
(
printed page 73383)
participating or competing in any horse show, exhibition, horse sale, or horse auction. In addition, any horses found to be sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations during actual participation in the show or exhibition, must be removed from further participation prior to the tyeing of the class or the completion of the exhibition. All horses tyed first in each TWH or racking horse class or event at any horse show or exhibition shall be inspected after being shown or exhibited to determine if such horses are sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations.
Paragraph (b) of § 11.20 also includes responsibilities for the management of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction which designates and appoints one or more DQPs to inspect horses. In such case, management must afford the DQP access to all records and areas of the grounds of such show, exhibition, sale, or auction, and the same right to inspect horses and records as is afforded to any APHIS representative, and must not take any action which would interfere with or influence a DQP in carrying out his or her duties or making decisions concerning whether or not any horse is sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations. This section also specifies procedures for management to follow should they be dissatisfied with a DQP's performance; identifies the horses DQPs must physically inspect at horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions and when DQPs must report alleged violations of the Act or regulations to management; and establishes the minimum number of DQPs that management must designate and appoint, based on the number of horses entered in an event. The regulations currently provide that management must appoint and designate at least 2 DQPs when more than 150 horses are entered.
Section 11.21 lists inspection procedures that DQPs must follow, including requirements for walking and turning the horse in a manner that allows the DQP to determine whether the horse exhibits signs of soreness. This section also includes the procedure for palpation to detect soreness, as well as procedures for conducting horses through other elements of the inspection process.
Under § 11.22, “Records required and disposition thereof,” the management of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, that contains TWHs or racking horses is required to maintain for at least 90 days following the closing date of the show, exhibition, or sale or auction, all pertinent records. If specifically required by APHIS, management may be required to hold the records specified longer than 90 days.
In § 11.23, “Inspection of records,” paragraph (a) states that the management of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction must allow any APHIS representative, upon request, to examine and make copies of any record pertaining to any horse. Similarly, paragraph (b) requires that HIOs that train, maintain, and license DQPs under a certified DQP program must permit any APHIS representative, upon request, to examine and copy any record relating to the DQP program that are required by any part of the regulations.
In § 11.24, “Reporting by management,” paragraph (a) states that within 5 days following the conclusion of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, containing TWHs or racking horses, management must submit to the Regional Director for the State in which the show, exhibition, sale or auction was held, information required in paragraphs (a)(1) through (a)(6) of § 11.22 for each horse excused or disqualified by management or its representatives from being shown, exhibited, sold or auctioned, and the reasons for such action. If no horses are excused or disqualified, the management shall submit a report so stating.
Paragraph (b) of § 11.24 states that within 5 days following the conclusion of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction which does not contain TWHs or racking horses, the management must inform the Regional Director for the State in which the show, exhibition, sale, or auction was held, of any case where a horse was excused or disqualified by management or its representatives from being shown, exhibited, sold or auctioned because it was found to be sore.
Section 11.25, “Minimum penalties to be assessed and enforced by HIOs that license DQPs,” lists suspensions and minimum penalties for violations of the Act and regulations. As discussed more fully below, although § 11.25 continues to appear in Part 11, USDA has been enjoined from enforcing this provision since 2015.
Contender Farms, L.L.P.
v.
U.S. Dep't of Agric.,
779 F.3d 258, 274 (5th Cir. 2015),
remanded sub nom. Show, Inc.
v.
U.S. Dep't of Agric., No. 4:12-cv-429, slip op. (N.D. Tex. Apr. 22, 2015)
(referred to in this docket as “
Contender Farms”
).
Sections 11.26 through 11.39 are currently omitted from Part 11. Section 11.40 lists prohibitions and requirements concerning persons involved in the transportation of certain horses, including providing APHIS with transportation information.
