Withdrawal of the 2024 Horse Protection Final Rule
In the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS recognized the potential for a legal challenge to the rule and considered the impact of vacatur of certain provisions of the rule. The Agency opined that “because the acceptance, training, and authorizing of HPIs may be accomplished in advance of the other provisions of the rule, the HPI-specific provisions of the rule do not depend on the other provisions, are capable of operating independently irrespective of the implementation of the other provisions, and are thus distinct and severable from these provisions. It is thus also the Agency's intent that, should a court hold any provisions of this rule to be invalid, such action shall not affect any other provision of this rule.” The Agency went on to provide several scenarios: “For example, should the rule's prohibitions on the use of pads, action devices, and toe extensions within the Tennessee Walking Horse and racking horse industry be removed, HPIs could still be trained and authorized regarding the remaining provisions of the rule, as well as the Act itself, and the Agency would still have jurisdiction over such training and authorization. Likewise, should the provisions regarding DCIS be removed, HPIs could still be trained and authorized regarding the remaining provisions of the rule, as well as the Act itself, and the Agency would still have jurisdiction over such training and authorization. Finally, should the HPI-specific provisions be removed and DQPs be retained, DQPs could still be trained and authorized regarding the remaining provisions of the rule and the Act itself.”
Although APHIS considered the impact of vacatur of certain provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, it underestimated the scope of the vacatur, which impacted not just one provision but four provisions of the rule, including provisions the Agency did not consider as part of its severability analysis: The procedures for appealing a disqualification resulting from an inspection conducted by an APHIS representative or an HPI and procedures for requesting a re-inspection of a horse (§ 11.5 and § 11.8(h)). Collectively, the U.S. District Court vacated the DCIS provision; the prohibitions on the use of pads, action devices, and substances on TWHs and racking horses; the provision establishing a process for appealing disqualifications based on inspection findings of APHIS representatives and HPIs; and the provision for requesting re-inspection by APHIS representatives and HPIs. Although APHIS initially intended to proceed with any non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, it did not anticipate the extent of the vacatur or the unworkable patchwork of provisions that would remain from the rule. Beyond this, the Agency did not anticipate the parallel litigation in
Gould
challenging the current regulations, or that Congress would not increase the HPA budget to provide funding necessary to implement the HPI program and the expanded scope of regulation under the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule. The District Court's broad vacatur resulted in gaps in the framework of the May 2024 Horse Protection rule. This vacatur, in combination with additional litigation and Congressional actions, has led us to reexamine the horse protection regulations in their entirety.
In considering appropriate next steps, we have carefully reviewed the House Appropriations Committee's report; prior rulemakings, public comments, and supporting analyses; the legislative and regulatory history of the HPA; APHIS' administration and enforcement of the Act; the horse industry's self-regulatory efforts; recommendations by the USDA Office of the Inspector General (OIG), the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NAS), the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), and the
(
printed page 73388)
American Association of Equine Practitioners (AAEP); and other horse sport oversight and inspection programs.
Like the House Appropriations Committee, APHIS has long recognized the need to communicate and work with the horse industry to eliminate soring so that individuals who carefully breed and patiently train their horses have a fair chance at competing in horse shows and exhibitions, and no horse is subjected to the cruel and inhumane practice of soring. Even before Congress enacted the HPA and assigned enforcement to USDA, concerns regarding soring initially led to self-regulatory efforts by the horse industry. It was only after these initial efforts failed to curb soring within the industry, and members of the horse industry and other organizations appealed to Congress for federal legislation, that Congress responded by passing the Horse Protection Act of 1970.
Although the original 1970 Act did not acknowledge the role of HIOs and third-party industry inspectors, USDA understood, from the beginning, that ending soring was a shared responsibility. For example, in the first set of regulations issued on February 1, 1972 (
37 FR 2426-2429
), the USDA included provisions to relieve management of liability if the sponsoring organization or show manager identified and removed sore horses before tying the class or the end of the exhibition, or the sponsoring organization designated a veterinarian to examine and observe all horses at the show or exhibition to determine whether such horses are sore. By 1973, the Tennessee Walking Horse Commission (a private organization that was composed of the Tennessee Walking Horse Breeders Association, Trainers' Association, and TWHNCA) required that their approximately 400 affiliated shows appoint show stewards to examine all horses before they compete and to exclude those that appear to be sore.
Horse Protection Enforcement, 1973-74, Biennial Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the United States Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
Congress reviewed the effects of the law against soring during oversight hearings in 1973. Testimony identified weaknesses in the Act that made enforcement difficult, particularly the Department's limited authority under the Act. By 1975, there was agreement among the Department, HIOs, and other organizations that the Act needed to be amended.
Horse Protection Enforcement, 1975-1976, Biennial Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the United States Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
Congress then amended the HPA in 1976 to make several important changes, including a provision that the USDA shall prescribe requirements for the appointment of persons qualified to inspect horses for the purpose of enforcing the Act.
In response to these amendments, on April 28, 1978, APHIS proposed to revise the HPA regulations (
43 FR 18514-18531
), and, in 1979, finalized this proposed rule in two stages ((
44 FR 1558-1566
, January 5, 1979) and (
44 FR 25172-25184
, April 27, 1979)). Among other changes, the revisions established a procedure to license DQPs to exclude sore horses on behalf of management, which was similar in design to the industry's self-regulatory efforts to use show stewards to inspect horses for signs of soring. Under the 1979 regulations, HIOs with established training programs certified by USDA to meet the purposes of the HPA could grant licenses to DQPs. Regarding the use of nonveterinarian inspectors, APHIS explained in the 1978 proposed rule that it was “the intent of Congress, when the 1976 Act was passed, for the Department to develop minimum qualification standards for nonveterinarians who may be retained by show management for the purpose of inspecting horses for compliance with the Act.” In the January 1979 final rule, APHIS went on to state that “a non-veterinarian DQP who is properly certified in accordance with 11.7 of the regulations should be fully qualified to detect and determine whether a horse is sore, as that term is defined in the Act” (
44 FR 1559
, January 5, 1979). This approach is consistent with other horse sport industries. Equestrian events across the spectrum—from Olympic disciplines like dressage and show jumping to breed-specific shows like Arabian and Quarter Horses—use industry stewards to monitor horse welfare and ensure a level playing field.
Almost immediately after implementing the DQP program, however, APHIS identified concerns regarding DQP performance. In its July 1980 report to Congress, APHIS stated that, “There indeed was evidence during 1979 that some DQP's were lax in excluding sore horses at shows not monitored by APHIS. APHIS officials insisted that the licensing organizations take responsibility for poor performance by DQP's and emphasized that certification would be withdrawn from organizations that do not police licensees properly.”
Horse Protection Enforcement, 1979, Annual Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the United States Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
In 1980, APHIS noted the rate of noncompliance identified by DQPs was 2.364 percent at shows monitored by APHIS, compared to 1.247 percent when APHIS was not present.
Horse Protection Enforcement, 1980, Annual Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the United States Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
This discrepancy between the rate of noncompliance identified by DQPs when APHIS is present and when it is not has continued throughout the entirety of the program. For example, in 1991, the average rate of noncompliance identified by DQPs was 2.220 percent at shows monitored by APHIS and 0.711 percent when APHIS was not present.
Horse Protection Enforcement, Fiscal Year 1991, Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
And, a September 2010 OIG audit report (Audit Report 33601-2-KC, referred to below as the OIG audit) found that, from 2005 to 2008, APHIS veterinarians were present at only 6 percent of all shows, yet DQPs identified 49 percent of all noncompliance with the HPA and regulations at that small percentage of shows where APHIS was present.
APHIS and others have explored various explanations to address this discrepancy over the years. In its 1980 report to Congress, APHIS opined that “part of the reason for this discrepancy may be that APHIS monitors primarily large events. At these events, more prizes, more money, and more prestige are at stake for participants and the competition is keener. Another reason may be that DQPs feel freer to act decisively when APHIS inspectors are present, providing visible support and protection from owners and trainers who might protest their decision.” On October 17, 1990, APHIS published a final rule in the
Federal Register
(
55 FR 41989-41994
, Docket No. 90-071) amending the regulations to expand and clarify the procedures for DQPs to follow when conducting inspections at horse shows, exhibitions, sales and auctions in response to concerns from both the horse industry and animal welfare organizations that the guidelines for preshow DQP examinations were not detailed enough to ensure uniform and adequate inspections of all horses examined by DQPs. On December 1, 1997, APHIS published a Horse
(
printed page 73389)
Protection Strategic Plan (
62 FR 63510
, Docket No. 97-105-1) to address the discrepancy in DQP inspection findings by partnering with HIOs on enforcement and holding HIOs accountable for the results of DQP inspections through program audits, uniform rules and sanctions, and proper training of DQPs. Following the publication of the strategic plan, APHIS and certified HIOs entered into annual/bi-annual operating plans for the implementation and enforcement of the Act from 1999 through 2009. Notably, despite the emphasis in the strategic plan to implement uniform rules and sanctions (including revoking the certification of an HIO or disqualifying a DQP from holding a license) and APHIS concerns about inspection discrepancies, available records indicate that USDA has only revoked the DQP program certification of two HIOs, and this action occurred in 1992.
Horse Protection Enforcement, Fiscal Year 1992, Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
Aside from these actions, USDA has not revised the regulatory framework for the DQP program or modernized DQP inspection procedures since 1979.
In August 2008, the AAEP's Tennessee Walking Horse Taskforce issued a white paper entitled, “Putting the Horse First: Veterinary Recommendations for Ending Soring of Tennessee Walking Horses,” which recommended ways to end soring. Among other things, the Taskforce recommended abolishment of the DQP program because of “conflicts of interest” in favor of APHIS Veterinary Medical Officers supervising a corps of veterinarians who would inspect walking horses using diagnostic tools and techniques for detecting noncompliant horses, such as thermography, digital radiography, drug testing, and swabbing for prohibited substances. While acknowledging the “significant financial resources” associated with implementing such a program, the Taskforce noted that “if the industry is serious in its intention to end this cruel and inhumane practice and restore the reputation of its breed and the integrity of its leadership, funding must be provided. The expense of these measures must be borne by the TWH industry.”
In 2010, the OIG audit found that DQPs were not always inspecting horses in accordance with the Act and regulations, including failing to observe the movement of horses during preshow inspection as required by § 11.21(a)(1), inspect horses tyed first in their class as required by § 11.21(b)(2)(iv), and report to management all of the horses the DQP identified as sore required by § 11.21(b)(3). The OIG audit report quoted an APHIS official as stating that that “these problems often occur because the DQPs come from within the horse show industry and are paid by the horse industry organizations. Therefore, they associate themselves much more closely with the needs of the exhibitors than with the horses they are there to protect.” The audit acknowledged that APHIS collaborated with the industry to implement the DQP program because its limited resources do not cover the costs of sending APHIS veterinarians to all HPA-covered events and it allows the industry and DQPs to serve as the “primary parties responsible for issuing immediate penalties to individuals for violating the Horse Protection Act,” when the Agency's own administrative enforcement “proceedings can be long, expensive, and have unpredictable results.” With respect to the audit, a then-APHIS official explained, “We're not able to attend all these shows with our funding right now, so we negotiated with the OIG auditors to (have the USDA) take over the training and licensing of the inspectors. We would then have full authority over training, licensing, and reprimanding of the DPQs [sic]. At this time, they're licensed under the horse industry organizations, and we are only able to recommend that a DQP be reprimanded[.]”
The Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, High time for change. Further USDA crackdown on soring practices expected, (March 2012).
Ultimately, the 2010 OIG audit report recommended that “APHIS abolish the DQP system and institute a system based on inspections by veterinarians independent of the horse industry.”
More recently, a 2021 NAS consensus study found that, as seen from 61 DQP inspection videos, DQPs did not carry out a sufficient observation of horse movement and that “differences in training and experience account for the discrepancies between VMO and DQP inspection results in past years. This discrepancy will continue to affect inspection outcomes if DQPs are not trained adequately and evaluated for competency by experienced equine veterinarians. Conflicts of interest may also influence decisions of DQPs in finding whether a horse is in compliance with the HPA.”
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. 2021. A Review of Methods for Detecting Soreness in Horses, Washington, DC: The National Academies Press
(referred to in this docket as the “NAS study”). The NAS study also concluded by stating that physical examination methods are critical in detecting pain “when performed by an examiner with sufficient knowledge of normal versus abnormal horse movement and posture and the ways that horses react to palpation if they are in pain. To better detect soreness it is important that these examinations be done thoroughly using proper techniques and used in conjunction with other diagnostic technologies, tools, and techniques.” As such, the NAS study authors “strongly recommend the use of DQPs for inspections be discontinued and that only veterinarians, preferably with equine experience, be allowed to examine horses, as is done in other equine competitions.”
In the August 2023 proposed rule that preceded the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS stated that, “as expressed by the USDA-OIG audit report and NAS study and supported by all major veterinary organizations, licensed veterinarians with equine experience are best qualified to detect soring in horses. Among other advantages, their medical training in anatomy and physiology affords them the ability to discern signs of soring in a horse that may be missed by experienced inspectors who lack such intensive training. In addition, licensed veterinarians in the United States are bound by their profession to ethical codes of conduct established by the AVMA and supported by other veterinary organizations. Under the AVMA principles for veterinary medical ethics, veterinarians are required to avoid conflicts of interest that put financial or other considerations ahead of animal welfare and the best interests of the animal involved.”
Ultimately, the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule removes the definition of HIO, explains that HIOs cannot have any involvement in any HPA-covered event, and replaces the DQP program with the HPI program by explaining, “HIOs are free to continue supplying other services to shows and events not subject to regulation, including registering participants and coordinating event logistics, supplying show judges, and promoting events . . . . [the] removal of the term was solely to reflect the fact that they would no longer have a distinct role specifically pertaining to APHIS' Horse Protection regulations.”
The May 2024 Horse Protection final rule then addresses the discrepancy in inspection findings by restricting third-party inspector eligibility to licensed veterinarians who are already ethically
(
printed page 73390)
bound to avoid conflicts of interest (except for veterinary technicians and persons employed by State and local government agencies to enforce laws or regulations pertaining to animal welfare who may be used if there is an insufficient pool of veterinarians) and providing that APHIS will assume responsibility for training the third-party inspectors. The rule makes APHIS representatives available to serve as functional equivalents to HPIs that may be appointed and retained by management—something neither OIG nor NAS recommended. Though the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule prioritizes the appointment of veterinarians as HPIs or APHIS representatives to perform inspections, it does not address concerns that the inspection procedures themselves and APHIS' administration of the Act contribute to the discrepancy in inspection findings; does not align with the Congressional statements behind the enactment of the 1976 HPA amendments, which, among other things, were intended to provide USDA and the industry with shared responsibilities for achieving the Act's purposes or the AAEP White Paper's overarching message that “the decision to develop realistic and effective means of eliminating individuals who perpetuate this culture [of soring] belongs to the TWH industry alone;” and does not describe how APHIS would carry out the HPI program (as supplemented with APHIS representatives) and expand the scope of regulation within the existing HPA budget if the funding increase to support implementation did not materialize.
For example, in response to the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, the TWHNCA submitted a public comment asserting that APHIS' data from 2017-2022 is unreliable because the data does not match prior publicly reported data and includes data of all noncompliance (not just soring). The TWHNCA also stated that the data “resulted from a subjective inspection process that has been shown to be incapable of producing repeatable results,” unless applied by experienced equine veterinarians. In addition, members of the horse industry have long raised statutory overreach and due process concerns involving the inspection program (as reflected in
Celebration, Gould,
and
Contender Farms
lawsuits), short-notice changes in inspection protocols at the start of show season, and changing enforcement strategies (including multiple rulemakings aimed at prohibiting the use of action devices and pads) that result in regulatory uncertainty for DQPs and HIOs, and owners, trainers, exhibitors, and the entire horse industry at large.
Over the years, both the scar rule and the re-inspection procedures have been sources of discrepancies in inspection findings between APHIS representatives and DQPs, and, as discussed above,
Gould
found these provisions deficient because they likely exceeded statutory authority and lacked adequate due process, respectively. Even before
Gould,
APHIS was aware of the industry's concerns that its re-inspection procedures lacked adequate due process,
McSwain
v.
Vilsack,
Case 1:16-cv-01234-RWS (Order, May 25, 2016), and, although the Agency temporarily adjusted its inspection procedures to ensure two APHIS Veterinary Medical Officers concurred on a finding of HPA noncompliance, it later reversed course.
In addition, when replacing the DQP program with the HPI program, in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS explained that “[b]eginning in 2010, APHIS undertook several nonregulatory approaches to help the industry improve compliance with the Act, among them increased engagement with industry groups, inspection workshops for DQPs, and stepped-up APHIS presence at certain shows to oversee inspections and check whether disqualified persons were participating.” These nonregulatory approaches also required HIOs to immediately update their rulebooks by December 1, 2010 (in advance of the current regulation's due date for updating rulebooks by March 1), extend the disqualification of a horse from a class to the entire event (which
Gould
subsequently found likely exceeded HPA statutory authority), impose minimum penalties for noncompliance with the HPA (which
Contender Farms
subsequently found likely exceeded HPA statutory authority), and, for the first time, begin identifying horses with a coffin bone rotation of more than 5 degrees as sore (even though such conditions could only be identified when APHIS attended events and included radiographs as part of its inspections), among other things.
“2010 Points of Emphasis,” Animal Care, APHIS USDA.
The May 2024 Horse Protection final rule also failed to address an important aspect of the problem: the inspection procedures themselves. The rule did not incorporate in the regulations any of the recommendations to enhance the inspection procedures to promote consistency among third-party inspectors or ensure that HPIs use current diagnostic tools, techniques, and tests consistent with advancements that have been implemented in other horse sport industries, including collecting blood samples to test for medications administered to horses to alter their response to palpation. Instead, the rule removed the inspection procedures currently found in § 11.21 from the regulations because “HIOs would no longer train DQPs in inspection procedures,” without regard for notice to individuals participating in covered events or the need for transparent regulatory procedures to which the HPIs could be held accountable.
In the August 2023 proposed rule, APHIS sought to address conflicts of interest by requiring veterinarian HPIs to hold an active license—ensuring they are bound by ethical standards—and by prohibiting HPI applicants, their immediate family members, and anyone providing them a financial benefit from participating in the showing, exhibition, sale, or auction of horses or from serving as a judge, farrier, or agent of management. However, the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule removed these safeguards, citing the national shortage of veterinarians as the reason for not finalizing the licensure requirement. It also removed the only horse-specific conflict-of-interest provision, stating that applying a “rigid regulatory qualification standard” without flexibility to assess individual circumstances could reduce the pool of eligible HPI applicants.
Instead of codifying provisions to address the conflicts of interest identified in the OIG audit and NAS study, the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule states that applicants will be asked to sign a code of conduct attesting to their freedom from “financial or professional” conflicts. Although the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule notes that APHIS will remove applicants and trainees from the program if conflicts are found, it does not establish regulatory criteria for denying an application or disqualifying an HPI on this basis, provide related due process procedures, or specify what constitutes a conflict of interest—an omission that contrasts with standard practice in other horse-sport organizations. For example, the Federation Equestre Internationale (FEI), the U.S. Equestrian Federation (USEF), the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Authority (HISA), and other equestrian bodies maintain detailed, publicly available conflict-of-interest policies for stewards and officials to ensure impartiality and the integrity of competition.
(
printed page 73391)
As it stands, the training and authorization of HPIs is the only provision from the 2024 Horse Protection final rule in effect. In the regulatory impact analysis or RIA that accompanied the 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS assumed that the rule would require the same number of HPIs as DQPs under the current regulations, which, at that time, was 59. Upon reflection, we believe APHIS may have underestimated the number of HPIs it would need to implement the 2024 Horse Protection final rule because the rule requires management to appoint two HPIs for shows or events when more than 100 horses are entered, when the current regulations require management to appoint two DQPs for shows or events when 150 horses are entered. Nevertheless, APHIS went on to explain that even though it estimated the rule would require 59 HPIs to serve as inspectors, it only anticipated receiving 30 applications per year for the HPI program and further acknowledged that it did not know the number of applicants who would meet regulatory requirements and be authorized to serve as HPIs. That is to say, from the inception of the HPI program, APHIS recognized that it would not draw an adequate pool of applicants to meet the projected needed for HPIs. Because of this shortfall in HPIs to serve as inspectors at over 200 covered events that occur each year, APHIS anticipated that it would need to expand its Animal Care Horse Protection program to make APHIS representatives available upon request by management to serve as inspectors, in addition to training and authorizing HPIs.
Despite accepting 67 applications from veterinarians, concerns remain about APHIS' ability to make inspectors available for more than 200 covered events. According to AAEP, veterinarians identifying as working with horses are a minority in the veterinary medical profession, estimated at 4,043 or 5.7 percent of the total number of private practice positions in the United States, with an additional 4,220 in mixed animal practice.
American Association of Equine Practitioners, Economic Report (April 1, 2019).
Combined, this means that less than 1 percent of potentially qualified veterinarians expressed interest in becoming HPIs. We believe this may be related to the salary expectations of veterinarians, who may earn significantly more providing their services in other evening and weekend shiftwork settings (including as relief veterinarians) than working as HPIs. Regardless of the reason, APHIS designed a program around the concept of veterinarians serving as the primary pool of inspectors and did not contemplate that less than 1 percent of potentially qualified veterinarians would be interested in the program. Even if APHIS had received funding to hire additional APHIS representatives to supplement the HPI program—which it did not, as discussed below—APHIS would still need to rely more heavily than planned on veterinary technicians and State and local government personnel who enforce animal welfare laws to provide coverage for over 200 events annually.
As noted above, the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule declined to codify any safeguards to address the conflict of interest identified in the OIG audit and NAS study. Instead, the rule indicates APHIS will ask applicants to sign a code of conduct attesting to their freedom from financial or professional conflicts of interest, without defining in the regulations what constitutes a conflict of interest or establishing regulatory procedures to deny an application or disqualify an HPI if a conflict is identified.
As alluded to above, there are budgetary concerns with implementing the 2024 Horse Protection final rule. In the regulatory impact analysis that accompanied the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS estimated that implementing the changes in the final rule would “result in additional costs to APHIS in terms of conducting inspections, screening, and training potential HPIs.” APHIS estimated that its costs under the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule could increase by up to $3.2 million annually. Year-to-year funding for the HPA program has, however, not increased since the issuance of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule; it has remained constant annually for FY 2024, 2025, and 2026. This means that the funding APHIS needs to implement the HPI program (including making APHIS representatives able to provide inspection services at HPA-covered events upon management's request) exceeds the current HPA budget.
Thus, although the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule implemented some of the recommendations in the OIG audit report and NAS study to discontinue the use of DQPs, the rule did not incorporate any of the recommendations from NAS or AAEP (or the industry itself) to improve the inspection procedures used to detect soreness to promote consistency across all HPA inspections; did not anticipate or consider the broad vacatur that could result from a legal challenge; did not include in the regulations conflict-of-interest provisions specific to horse protection activities; and did not consider that APHIS may not receive an increase in funding to enable APHIS representatives to serve as third-party inspectors (even though both the OIG audit report and the NAS study acknowledged APHIS' limited HPA budget). With regard to the NAS study, the authors explained, “If the limited budget for HPA enforcement necessitates continued use of third-party inspectors, the committee recommends that they should be veterinarians or equine industry professionals who are screened for potential conflicts of interest and that they be trained to inspect by APHIS, not by HIOs. . . . Training should be done by experienced equine veterinarians, and strict competency evaluations should be conducted to assess the skills and knowledge of trainees before they are given license to inspect horses. Consequences for performing a substandard examination should be strictly enforced and reports of substandard performance and letters of admonishment should come from the APHIS, not HIOs.”
After careful consideration, as recommended by the House Appropriations Committee, we propose a path forward that allows the Agency to better address the root causes of the identified deficiencies in the DQP program and to implement recommendations from AAEP, OIG, and NAS related to third-party inspector conflicts of interest; the NAS study findings and recommendations concerning the need for adequate training and evaluation of third-party inspectors; the recommendations by NAS and AAEP to use diagnostic technologies, tools, and techniques in conjunction with physical examinations consistent with other horse sports; and alignment of the Horse Protection program with the intent of the HPA. Finally, we are mindful of the intent of the 1976 amendments to the HPA. When President Ford signed the 1976 amendments into law, he stated he was “committed to achieving meaningful reform by compelling this industry to police itself properly,” and his Administration promised to work “to gain greater support from within the industry for self-policing and compliance with the Department's expanded program.”
Statement on Signing the Horse Protection Act Amendments of 1976, 3 PUB. PAPERS 1999, 2013 (July 14, 1976)
and
Memorandum for the President from
(
printed page 73392)
James M. Frey at 5, Office of Management and Budget (July 8, 1976)
(recommending President Ford approve the HPA amendments because “the key to a successful program centers around industry involvement”).
In keeping with this promise and the intent and history of the HPA, we propose to withdraw the non-vacated portions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule and propose changes to the current regulations that more fully address the recommendations of OIG, AAEP, and NAS, support the industry's self-regulatory efforts and alignment with other horse sports, and modernize the inspection procedures in the regulations for the first time in 34 years. As part of this proposed rule and as discussed below, we would ensure that DQPs are screened for conflicts of interest to ensure objective inspection outcomes, trained and evaluated for competency by experienced equine veterinarians, and regularly monitored to ensure required inspection procedures are followed and inspections are performed consistently, whether APHIS is present or not.

The 2024 Horse Protection final rule amended § 11.6(a) to add a general prohibition on the use of any device, method, practice, or substance that can be used to “mask previous or ongoing soring.” In light of the vacatur of the DCIS provision in

Therefore, we are proposing to withdraw this provision of the final rule. However, we continue to find that the use of agents used to mask ongoing soring is a serious violation of the HPA and propose related changes to the regulations in this proposed rule, as discussed below.
Paragraph (b) of § 11.6 of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule lists specific prohibitions regarding action devices, equipment, or practices on any horse at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction. Most of the prohibitions in that section were drawn from existing provisions in § 11.2 of the current regulations; § 11.2 of the current regulations is still in effect and operative; hence retaining the parallel provisions from § 11.6 of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule would be redundant and unnecessary.
Section 11.6(b)(9) and (b)(10) of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule also replaced “yearling horses” with “horses up to 2 years old.” There is no need to define “yearling horse” as a “horse up to 2 years old” since this term is understood in the industry to mean a horse up to 2 years old. The rule also amended the existing regulation by specifying that, for horses up to 2 years old, kegs or similar conventional horseshoes must weigh 16 ounces or less; however, this is duplicative of what is in the current rule (§ 11.2(b)(9)) because the current rule already prohibits any horseshoe on yearling horses that weighs more than 16 ounces. Therefore, we are proposing to withdraw this provision.
Paragraphs 11.6(b)(14) and (b)(19) of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule included prohibitions on acrylic and hardening substances as hoof packing, paring of the frog or sole, and bruising of the hoof or any other method of pressure shoeing. The use of acrylic and hardening substances as hoof packing, paring of the frog or sole, and bruising of the hoof are all examples of pressure shoeing. Current § 11.2(b)(18) already prohibits pressure shoeing of any kind. When proposing the current § 11.2(b)(18), the Agency explained that its purpose was to prohibit all practices that could result in pressure shoeing: “The Horse Protection Act Amendments of 1976 specifically prohibit any practice involving the limb of a horse that results in the horse suffering, or can reasonably be expected to result in the horse suffering pain, distress, inflammation, or lameness when walking, trotting, or otherwise moving. Consequently, the Department proposes to prohibit the shoeing or trimming of a horse's hoof in a manner that will cause such horse to suffer pain, distress, or inflammation when walking, trotting, or otherwise moving. Consequently, Department officials believe this prohibition is necessary to protect horses from unscrupulous horsemen and farriers who engage in practices such as, but not limited to, placing a pressure wedge between the shoe pad and the frog; deliberately trimming the hoof without properly trimming the sole, thereby causing the sole to act as a pressure plate; placing a tack or screw in the shoe pad in such a manner that it will slightly penetrate the frog of the horse's foot; and, deliberately “quicking” the hoof of a horse with the horseshoe nails.”

However, rather than providing greater clarity, the Tech Note caused further confusion and concern, as compliance would require management of all other horse events to notify APHIS of their events, regardless of whether the breed or discipline has historically been subject to the practice of soring, including any score-based event, such as 4H Club events, Cart/Driving classes, Costume classes, Dressage events, Equitation, Pleasure classes, Halter/Showmanship, Hunter, Hunter Under Saddle, Polo, Ranch Horse Versatility, Ranch Riding, Reining, Trail classes, and Vaulting. Proposed Revisions to the Current Regulations

Administrator, APHIS,
APHIS representative, APHIS Show Veterinarian,
Department, Regional Director,
and

from § 11.1 and referring to them by the general term

which means “any employee of APHIS, or any officer or employee of any State agency who is authorized by the Administrator to perform inspections or any other functions authorized by the Act, including the inspection of the records of any horse show, horse exhibition, horse sale or horse auction.”

Prohibitions Concerning Exhibitors (§ 11.2)
Section 11.2, “Prohibitions concerning exhibitors,” lists general and specific prohibitions for any device, method, practice, or substance used on any horse at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, competition restrictions for 2-year-old TWHs and racking horses, and information requirements under the Act and regulations.
Under the current regulations, paragraph (b)(17) of § 11.2 prohibits the use of “any action device or any other device that strikes the coronet band of the foot of a horse except for soft rubber or soft leather bell boots that are used as protective devices.” When this requirement was proposed in 1978, APHIS explained that the intent was to prohibit devices “from being placed on a horse's leg in a manner that will allow such device to strike the coronet band of a horse's foot while such horse is in motion or at rest.”
Although the intent of this requirement has been clear for decades, APHIS representatives have received questions regarding whether chains and other devices must be fitted to avoid landing on or striking any location around the circumference of the coronet band. To reaffirm the intent of the requirement, we are proposing to clarify that the device cannot strike “any location on” the coronet band of the foot of the horse when the horse is in motion or at rest. Thus, for purposes of HPA inspections, the APHIS representative or
(
printed page 73396)
DQP will evaluate any chain or action device placed on a horse to ensure it does not land on or strike any location around the circumference of the coronet band. To ensure this evaluation occurs during DQP inspections, we would also add a conforming change to the inspection procedures in § 11.21.
Since the 1970s, the Department has been concerned about the veracity of inspections under the HPA due to the use of medications and other substances that conceal soring in TWHs and racking horses. For example, in its 1975-1976 report to Congress, the Department explained that “new and devious means” are being used to sore horses that are difficult to detect and that “anti-inflammatory agents and painkillers are used to mask soring.” Calling the practice of soring “one of the most significant welfare issues affecting any equine breed or discipline,” the AAEP's 2008 White Paper recommended that APHIS adopt drug testing based on the methodology and practices established by the USEF and swabbing of limbs to test for the presence of prohibited substances using current standard methodology.
In 2014, the TWHNCA created a veterinary advisory committee (VAC) that oversaw the collection and testing of blood samples taken from TWHs during the 2014, 2015, and 2016 National Celebrations to determine compliance with medication withdrawal guidelines set by the VAC. According to the NAS study, “one of the documents provided by the TWH industry representative, the number of samples taken in 2014, 2015, and 2016 were 407, 88, and 84, respectively. Of these samples 230, 88, and 26 were selected for testing. The numbers of samples that tested positive for prohibited medications were 51 out of 230 in 2014, 0 out of 88 in 2015, and 17 (9 were from pleasure horses) out of 26 in 2016. In 2014 the medications most prevalent in the samples were methylprednisolone, a steroid primarily used for treating joint and soft tissue inflammation (26 samples); triamcinolone acetonide, a corticosteroid for treating skin and joint conditions (14 samples); and diclofenac, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) (12 samples). Some samples were found to contain at least two anti-inflammatory medications. The results of the testing in 2015 indicated that all samples were in compliance with the VAC's medication withdrawal guidelines. In 2016 some samples were found to be noncompliant with withdrawal guidelines for some compounds, namely romifidine, a sedative; phenylbutazone, an NSAID; and stanozonol, a synthetic steroid with anabolic and androgenic properties.” Similarly, APHIS' own blood samples from 80 horses at 6 horse shows in 2015 found that 20 percent of those horses tested positive for sedatives or NSAIDs.
The NAS study reviewed the methods of detecting soring in horses. Based on its review, the NAS study recommended that APHIS adopt blood testing as a component of its process for evaluating horses for compliance with the HPA. In making this recommendation, the NAS study cited research indicating that NSAIDs, opioids, and local anesthetics may “abolish a sore horse's response to palpation by decreasing mechanical nociceptive thresholds to palpation.” In addition, topically applied substances can be used to mask inflammation (
e.g.,
redness of skin, edema of the skin, and loss of skin integrity).
As discussed in the NAS study, blood sampling to test for prohibited medications and medications conditionally permitted but given above therapeutic levels is common in horse sports around the world to protect horse welfare and to ensure fair competition. Testing is done according to medication rules and guidelines set by a regulatory body, based on data on how the use or overuse of these medications can adversely affect the horse or alter its performance. For example, the USEF has established a protocol for testing and a policy on prohibited drugs and permitted medications, including concentrations allowed for permitted medications. However, the current regulations do not require blood testing as a component of the process followed by DQPs for evaluating horses for compliance with the HPA. Although APHIS has collected and tested blood samples from horses at some of the HPA-covered events it has attended, to achieve the dual purposes of the Act, it is critically important that the inspection process is consistent at all covered events.
In recent years, APHIS representatives have observed an increase in horses exhibiting signs of sedation during inspection. APHIS has found syringes and containers with sedatives and other prohibited substances in the warmup area and during barn walks, and been made aware of DQPs removing syringes from the warmup area and of individuals using syringes to inject reversal agents in horses in the warmup area after inspection, so that horses that pass inspection may suffer physical pain or distress while being shown and compete unfairly with horses that are not sore. In addition, we anticipate one of the changes proposed in this rulemaking may increase the use of medications and substances to mask soring. Specifically, as discussed below, we intend to clarify that, due to the Court's preliminary decision in
Gould,
management must disqualify any horse which is sore only from participating or competing in the class in which the horse was inspected for entry, showing, exhibition, sale or auction, or being offered for purchase. This change would allow the horse to be presented for inspection in a subsequent class of an event (whether later in the day or on a different day for a multi-day event) after being disqualified by management from a previous class at the same horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction. Individuals wishing to conceal signs of soring to pass preshow inspection in subsequent classes may try to apply masking agents to a horse's pasterns or sedate the horse to alter its response to palpation and compete unfairly with horses that are not sore. The use of medications and substances that mask soring during inspection directly interferes with the primary mechanism of enforcement under the Act, causes DQPs and APHIS representatives to make false entries or statements in required reports and records because the use of such masking agents may interfere with accurate inspection findings, and constitutes a grave violation of the Act.
Relatedly, although the current regulations contain prohibitions on substances, the regulations do not require swabbing to test for prohibited substances as a component of the process that DQPs must follow for evaluating horses for compliance with the Act and regulations, including for those substances that conceal signs of soring. Swabs collected by APHIS during its inspections have regularly detected prohibited substances, including a high prevalence of prohibited substances on padded horses. For example, APHIS continued to detect analgesic and anesthetic agents throughout FYs 2017-2023. Of these agents, Benzocaine and Lidocaine were the primary agents detected by laboratory analysis, with Camphor, Diclofenac, Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO), and Menthol also being detected. The average percentage of swabs over this 7-year period that tested positive for these agents was 37 percent. Performance horses overwhelmingly accounted for the horses that tested positive for prohibited substances, consisting of 90.4 percent of horses testing positive during that period. Additionally, the average percentage of performance horses sampled that tested positive for a prohibited substance during fiscal years 2017-2023 was 35.2
(
printed page 73397)
percent. Although APHIS swabs horses for prohibited substances at some of the HPA-covered events it attends, to achieve the dual purposes of the Act, it is critically important that the inspection process is consistent at all events.
For these reasons, and to promote consistency of the inspection process at all HPA-covered events, we propose to revise paragraphs (c) and (e) of this section to make clear that the use of masking agents (such as, but not limited to, sedatives or topical numbing agents) and other substances that conceal evidence of soring are prohibited. Specifically, paragraph (c) of this section currently prohibits all substances, except for lubricants used under certain conditions, on the extremities above the hoof on any TWH or racking horse while being shown, exhibited, or offered for sale at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction. Notably, requirements depart from the prohibition on the use of substances in the HPA in two respects: (1) In addition to prohibiting the showing, exhibition, sale, and auction of horses wearing or bearing prohibited substances, the HPA also prohibits the entering of such horses; and (2) the HPA authorizes the USDA to prohibit substances to prevent the soring of horses.
To better align § 11.2(c) of the regulations with the HPA and for the reasons discussed above, we would revise this paragraph to narrow the list of prohibited substances applicable to Tennessee Walking Horses and racking horses to only those that cause or can reasonably be expected to cause any horse to be sore or that mask or can reasonably be expected to mask evidence of soring. Examples of substances that can mask or reasonably be expected to mask evidence of soring include sedatives, topically applied numbing agents, and topically applied substances that mask inflammation (
e.g.,
redness of skin, edema of the skin, and loss of skin integrity). Prohibiting substances that can mask or are reasonably expected to mask evidence of soring is necessary to prevent the soring of horses. In addition, we would continue to prohibit the application of all substances on the extremities above the hoof of any TWH or racking horse after the horse has been inspected by management or by a DQP, except that lubricants such as glycerine, petrolatum, and mineral oil, or mixtures thereof may be used if management agrees to furnish the lubricants, maintain control over them, and the use otherwise meets the conditions of the regulations.
In addition, we are proposing to revise the horse-related information requirements under § 11.2(e). Paragraph (e) currently prohibits “[f]ailing to provide information or providing any false or misleading information required by the Act or regulations or requested by Department representatives, by any person that owns, trains, shows, exhibits, or sells or has custody of, or direction or control over any horse shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned or entered for the purpose of being shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned at any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction[.]” The current regulations list examples of such information, including “Information concerning the registered name, markings, sex, age, and legal ownership of the horse; the name and address of the horse's training and/or stabling facilities; the name and address of the owner, trainer, rider, any other exhibitor, or other legal entity bearing responsibility for the horse; the class in which the horse is entered or shown; the exhibitor identification number; and, any other information reasonably related to the identification, ownership, control, direction, or supervision of any such horse.”
In paragraph (e), we are proposing to prohibit the use of masking agents (such as, but not limited to, sedatives or topical numbing agents) and other substances that conceal evidence of soring that may cause false entry or statement in a report or other record required under the Act or regulations. This proposed change is consistent with the proposed § 11.2(c), which also prohibits the use of masking agents under Section 1824(7) of the HPA. As discussed below, we are also proposing related changes in §§ 11.4, 11.7, and 11.21 of the regulations to ensure regular blood testing and swabbing of horses at covered events in accordance with the uniform inspection procedures of the DQP's certified organization or association, and otherwise make clear that horses that are sore may not be presented for inspection in a manner that might cause the horse not to respond to inspection by DQPs or APHIS representatives. These prohibitions are narrowly tailored to prevent the soring of horses.
In addition, we would also make changes to paragraph (e) for clarity. The information required in paragraph (e) is necessary for enforcing the Act. In the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, we supplemented the horse-related information requirements to expand the examples of individuals who must provide information required by the Act or regulations or requested by APHIS to include any person who enters or transports any horse shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned in HPA-covered events, and specified that such individuals must not provide any false or misleading information. Our proposed revisions in this rule would incorporate the persons included in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule and would further clarify the list of individuals who must follow the requirements by generalizing it to all persons subject to the Act and regulations. This is because there are other entities that have horse-related information responsibilities under the Act and regulations. Specifically, management of horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions, DQPs, and HIOs with certified DQP programs are also required to provide information related to horses. Failing to do so, or providing false or misleading information, is prohibited by law. Moreover, Section 1825(a)(2)(B) of the HPA prohibits anyone from knowingly making, or causing to be made, false statements or records required under the HPA or regulations, and to knowingly cause another person to do the same. To more fully capture the horse-related information requirements that individuals must provide to APHIS under the HPA and regulations, we propose to revise this paragraph by stating that failing to provide information, providing any false or misleading information, or causing another person to provide false or misleading information required by the Act or regulations or requested by APHIS representatives to enforce the Act or regulations is prohibited regardless of the party doing so. We would retain the examples of information related to identification, ownership, control, direction, and supervision of horses, and add that such information would also include information bearing on compliance with the requirements of the Act or regulations. To be clear, the net result of these proposed changes simply affirms what is already required by law; that is, persons must provide truthful and accurate information required by the Act or regulations or upon request by APHIS representatives.
Scar Rule (§ 11.3)
Under current § 11.3 of the regulations, all horses subject to the “scar rule” that do not meet certain criteria are considered sore and are subject to all prohibitions of section 5 of the Act. Paragraph (a) states that “the anterior and anterior-lateral surfaces of the fore pasterns (extensor surface) must be free of bilateral granulomas, other bilateral pathological evidence of inflammation, and, other bilateral
(
printed page 73398)
evidence of abuse indicative of soring including, but not limited to, excessive loss of hair.” A footnote is also appended to paragraph (a). It defines “granuloma” as “any one of a rather large group of fairly distinctive focal lesions that are formed as a result of inflammatory reactions caused by biological, chemical, or physical agents.”
Paragraph (b) of the scar rule states that “the posterior surfaces of the pasterns (flexor surface), including the sulcus or “ `pocket' ” may show bilateral areas of uniformly thickened epithelial tissue if such areas are free of proliferating granuloma tissue, irritation, moisture, edema, or other evidence of inflammation.”
In paragraph (a)(2) of § 11.21, the requirements for inspection of horses by DQPs include an examination to determine whether the horse meets the scar rule criteria. Paragraph (a)(2) states that “[w]hile carrying out the procedures set forth in this paragraph, the DQP shall also inspect the horse to determine whether the provisions of § 11.3 of this part are being complied with, and particularly whether there is any evidence of inflammation, edema, or proliferating granuloma tissue.”
Long before the scar rule was added to the regulations in 1979, the organized horse industry had agreed that bilateral scars on the front pasterns are clear evidence that a horse has been sored. By 1974, the Tennessee Walking Horse Commission established its own scar rule, “under which scarred horses 2 years old were supposed to be excluded from competition. The rule was to be expanded to include 3-year-olds in 1975, 4-years-olds in 1976, and so on incrementally in future years.”
Horse Protection Enforcement, 1979: Annual Report of the Secretary of Agriculture to the President of the United States Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
Despite this effort, the industry's rule was not applied uniformly and “young horses new to competition continued to be entered with scars on the pasterns.”
As a result, the horse industry said it would support a uniform, nationwide scar rule, and APHIS established the scar rule in the regulations for all horses foaled during or after 1976. By applying the scar rule only to horses born and trained after the 1976 amendments to the HPA, APHIS explained in its 1979 final rule that these horses should have no scars at all if the law is being followed.
Even though more than a generation of horses have come and gone since the scar rule was first introduced, some horses entered in horse shows and other covered events continue to show evidence indicative of soring. As training techniques have changed over the past 47 years, so too has the appearance of inflammation associated with soring practices and “scar” does not accurately describe the pathological evidence of inflammation and other changes that appear on some horses today. As part of the NAS study, a board-certified veterinary pathologist reviewed 24 pairs of skin samples taken from TWHs that had been disqualified for noncompliance with the scar rule at the 2015 and 2016 National Celebrations and found pathological changes indicative of repeated trauma that correlated to the unnatural thickening of the skin visible on gross examination.
In the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS revised the scar rule based on recommendations from the NAS study and advances in veterinary science and technical innovations in imaging and diagnostics that have improved our understanding of how soring occurs and our ability to detect it. The revised scar rule, referred to as the DCIS provision, provided that: “The forelimbs and hindlimbs of the horse must be free of dermatologic conditions that are indicative of soring. Examples of such dermatologic conditions include, but are not limited to, irritation, moisture, edema, swelling, redness, epidermal thickening, loss of hair (patchy or diffuse) or other evidence of inflammation. Any horse found to have one or more of the dermatologic conditions set forth herein shall be presumed to be `sore' and be subject to all prohibitions of section 6 (
15 U.S.C. 1825
) of the Act.”
As noted above, in
Celebration,
the court vacated the DCIS provisions of the May 2024 HPA final rule. Additionally, on August 19, 2025, the same court in
Gould
found that the existing scar rule likely exceeds statutory authority because “a horse could be disqualified as sore under the Scar rule without any proof of specific misconduct of soring” and “evidence of past soring is not—and should not be—a basis for a horse not found to be currently sore.” In so ruling, the court concluded that plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the existing scar rule exceeds the HPA statutory authority. Regarding the DCIS provision in the May 2024 final rule, the court in
Celebration
vacated the regulation because it lacked clear standards for what dermatologic conditions would disqualify a horse and, thus, failed to provide owners and trainers with adequate due process.
We are proposing to remove the scar rule from the current regulations based on the court's preliminary finding that evidence of past soring cannot be used as a basis for finding a horse sore at the time of inspection. We would continue to apply the statutory definition of “sore” when evaluating horses for compliance with the HPA, including identifying horses that exhibit inflammation (such as redness and swelling) associated with soring practices.
Although we are removing the scar rule from the current regulations, we plan to reserve § 11.3. We are not proposing a new replacement to the existing scar rule at this time because we are undertaking additional study, as recommended by the NAS study, to, among other things, determine if “training practices that can cause soreness in TWHs also result in lichenification” and “epidermal thickening (hyperplasia) and lichenification are solely caused by the action devices worn by TWHs.” As noted in the NAS study, the skin changes seen on the pasterns of TWHs “are not observed on the pasterns of other breeds of horses (Arabians, American Saddlebreds, Morgan horses), which also train with action devices such as chains and rollers but do not wear them when shown at competitions. Action devices used in other breeds are not limited by weight and usually of lower weight than those used in TWHs. Walking horses are often trained with action devices weighing in excess of the 6-ounce action devices currently allowed for competition. The use of heavier or more cumbersome devices in training may be more likely to contribute to the formation of the lesions” seen on the pasterns of TWHs. Additional study will enable APHIS to better understand the physiological and dermatological changes associated with the use of action devices to train TWHs and racking horses, and whether it is possible to develop a regulatory provision like the scar rule that aligns with the HPA's statutory authority, can be consistently applied, and effectively conveys clear standards for dermatologic conditions that are indicative of present soreness.
In the meantime, as noted above, the horse industry enforced its own scar rule long before the USDA added it to the regulations in 1979. As such, the industry—through show managers, HIO leadership, judges, owners, trainers, farriers, riders, and exhibitors of horses—could again decide to align on self-regulation to address the issue of horses that bear scars and other evidence of past abuse indicative of soring to ensure fair competition for individuals who carefully breed and patiently train their horses.

Inspection of Horses by APHIS (§ 11.4)
In this section, we are proposing to make two substantive changes. First, we are proposing to add a provision to paragraph (b) to ensure that the person having custody of the horse during an inspection by an APHIS representative does not interfere with the examination procedures. Since 1990, the inspection procedures for DQPs in § 11.21(a)(4) have provided that the DQP shall instruct the person having custody of the horse to control it by holding the reins approximately 18 inches from the bit shank and that a horse shall not be inspected if whips, cigarette smoke, or other actions or paraphernalia are used to distract the horse during examination. We propose to incorporate these same requirements during an inspection by an APHIS representative. In conformance with proposed § 11.2, we would also add the use of masking agents, such as but not limited to sedatives or topical numbing agents, to the list of actions and paraphernalia that may not be used to cause the horse not to respond to APHIS' examination. It is our intent to prohibit any activities that interfere in any way with the proper and reliable identification of a sore horse.
Specifically, the proposed addition to paragraph (b) would state: “During the inspection, the person having custody of the horse shall control the horse by holding the reins approximately 18 inches from the bit shank. Such person shall not present the horse in a manner that might cause the horse not to respond to APHIS' examination, including use of masking agents (such as, but not limited to, sedatives or topical numbing agents), whips, cigarette smoke, or other actions or paraphernalia to distract the horse during examination.”
Second, we propose to revise the procedures for reexamination of horses allegedly found to be in violation of the Act or regulations by an APHIS representative. Currently, the regulations in § 11.4(h) provide that the owner, trainer, exhibitor, or other person having custody of such a horse may request reexamination and testing of the horse within a 24-hour period, provided such request is made to the APHIS Show Veterinarian immediately after the horse has been examined by APHIS representatives and before the horse is removed from the inspection area. The APHIS Show Veterinarian will reexamine the horse if he or she determines that sufficient cause for reexamination exists and the horse is maintained under APHIS supervisory custody during the reexamination.
As discussed above, the U.S. District Court in
Gould
issued an order preliminarily enjoining enforcement against plaintiffs of the “disqualification rules that fail to provide adequate due process” in the current regulations, and in
Celebration,
it vacated the reexamination and appeal procedures in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule.
To address the deficiencies with the reexamination and appeal procedures, we are proposing two interlocking mechanisms to ensure adequate pre-deprivation review of findings by an APHIS representative that a horse is allegedly in violation of the Act or regulations before notification to management for purposes of disqualifying or excusing the horse from competition. First, we would revise the reexamination procedure in current § 11.4 to require a second APHIS veterinarian to independently inspect the horse. Thus, two APHIS veterinarians who independently inspected the horse must concur on a finding of an alleged violation of the Act or regulations before notifying the person having custody of the horse of the alleged violation.
As noted, the two APHIS veterinarians must concur as to the type of finding. If one APHIS veterinarian found the horse sore and the other APHIS veterinarian found an equipment noncompliance, they would not “concur” on a finding. Alternatively, if one APHIS veterinarian found the horse bilaterally sore on the forelimbs and the other APHIS veterinarian found the horse unilaterally sore on a forelimb, they would concur on the finding of a unilateral sore horse. This approach is consistent with FEI Sports Limb Sensitivity Testing Procedure. As noted in the NAS study, the FEI procedure provides that “[a]ll veterinarians and the ground jury must agree that the horse shows altered sensitivity, although they do not have to agree on precisely where the horse is sensitive.” By requiring two APHIS veterinarians to concur as to type of finding, this proposed provision would remove the APHIS Show Veterinarian's discretion to grant or deny a request for reexamination based on their determination of whether sufficient cause for reexamination exists and alleviate the burden of requesting a reexamination on the part of the person having custody of or responsibility for the horse.
To be clear, we are proposing these revisions to the reexamination procedures specifically to address the due process concerns identified by the U.S. District Court in
Gould
and
Celebration.
APHIS representatives who conduct inspections at covered events are highly trained, experienced veterinarians who follow established examination protocols to assess compliance with the HPA and its regulations. While inspections conducted by APHIS veterinarians are reliable, the NAS study highlighted limitations in prior procedures requiring two APHIS veterinarians to concur on findings of noncompliance. As the NAS noted, these procedures may not account for changes that can occur between examinations, the horse's response to repeated palpation, or the influence of prohibited substances—whether applied parenterally or topically—on findings over time.
However, given the court's due process concerns, we believe it is necessary to adopt clear, standardized, and nondiscretionary reexamination procedures that ensure owners, trainers, exhibitors, and other persons having responsibility for a horse receive adequate pre-deprivation process. We recognize that this approach may introduce some risk that a horse could respond differently between examinations by APHIS veterinarians, but we conclude that the benefit of providing procedural protections outweighs the potential for changes in a horse's response that could lead APHIS veterinarians to reach different findings. In addition to requiring two APHIS veterinarians to independently inspect any horse allegedly in violation of the Act or regulations, we would also allow the owner, trainer, exhibitor, or other person having custody of or responsibility for the horse the opportunity to appeal the finding to a qualified Appeals Official before the horse is removed from the inspection area (the qualifications of Appeals Officials is discussed in “Qualifications of Appeals Officials (§ 11.8),” below).
The Appeals Official would be responsible for independently reviewing the evidence or facts offered by the person who submitted the appeal and APHIS, considering the relevance, reliability, and credibility of such evidence and information, and applying the provisions of the Act and the regulations. Following his or her review, the Appeals Official may set aside the APHIS inspection finding or affirm the finding in whole or in part, while taking care to make his or her decision expeditiously so as not to delay or interrupt individual classes or performances at the horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction. At the event, the Appeals Official would provide an oral decision on the appeal
(
printed page 73400)
to APHIS and the person who submitted the appeal.
Under this proposal, APHIS would only notify management of a horse allegedly found in violation of the Act or the regulations if: (1) The two inspecting APHIS veterinarians independently inspected the horse and concur on the finding of an alleged violation of the Act or the regulations, and no appeal was submitted before the horse was removed from the APHIS inspection area; or (2) the Appeals Official provided an oral decision affirming, in whole or in part, the finding of an alleged violation or violations of the Act or the regulations.
Certification and Licensing of DQPs (§ 11.7)
Section 11.7, “Certification and licensing of designated qualified persons (DQP's),” sets forth the qualifications and requirements for DQPs and DQP programs. Paragraph (a) of § 11.7, “Basic qualifications of DQP applicants,” lists basic professional qualifications required of DQP applicants and paragraph (b) lists certification requirements for DQP programs certified by the Department and initiated and maintained by HIOs. As part of maintaining a certified DQP program, HIOs are responsible for delivering the training curriculum as well as ensuring that criteria for selecting and licensing DQPs are met. In addition, paragraphs (c) and (d) establish licensing requirements for DQPs and requirements that must be met by DQPs and HIOs. Finally, paragraphs (e), (f), and (g) establish prohibitions on the appointment of certain persons to detect and diagnose horses which are sore or to otherwise inspect horses for the purpose of enforcing the Act, and procedures for cancelling DQP licenses and revoking DQP program certifications of HIOs, respectively.
In this section, we propose changes to address the root causes of discrepancies in inspections: Third-party inspector qualifications, third-party inspector training and oversight, and the thoroughness and consistency of inspection procedures. First, based on recommendations from the OIG audit report and NAS study regarding DQP performance, we propose changes related to:
Conflict of interest—DQPs should be screened for conflicts of interest to ensure objective inspection outcomes.
Training and evaluation—DQPs should be trained and evaluated for competency by experienced equine veterinarians.
Performance monitoring—DQP performance should be monitored to ensure inspection procedures are followed and inspections are performed consistently, whether APHIS is present at the event or not.
Second, we propose changes to enhance the certification requirements for DQP programs and strengthen the inspection procedures that will occur at HPA-covered events. As noted above, in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS removed all HPA enforcement-related responsibilities from HIOs and restricted HIOs from providing services at events that fall under the regulations. This means that, if APHIS were to retain the HPI program, APHIS would have to fund enhancements to the inspection process (which would be cost prohibitive), continue to use enhanced inspection techniques on an event-by-event basis (which has led to the inconsistencies and discrepancies in inspection findings), or make no changes to the inspection process and, thus, not address important aspects of the problem related to the adequacy of inspections at HPA-covered events (which is the course the Agency took in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule). By retaining and enhancing the certification requirements for DQP programs, APHIS can address recommendations from TWHNCA's VAC Report,

1

the AAEP's White Paper on Putting the Horse First, and the NAS study to improve the HPA inspection procedures at HPA-covered events.
All three groups have stressed the need for consistent inspection procedures at HPA-covered events that align more closely with inspection procedures used in other horse sports, such as blood testing to test for sedatives and improved testing for topical prohibited substances. Although APHIS has, at times, tested blood samples and swabs for prohibited substances and used diagnostic techniques, such digital radiography, when carrying out HPA compliance inspections, APHIS has not modernized the DQP inspection procedures in the regulations that apply at all HPA-covered events since 1992. When APHIS and third-party inspectors use different techniques to assess horses for compliance with the HPA, it results in variability in inspection, discrepancies in inspection findings, and inconsistent application of the HPA. For these reasons, APHIS is proposing changes to enhance the certification requirements for DQP programs and strengthen the HPA inspection procedures.
Basic Qualifications of DQP Applicants
Section 11.7(a) of the current regulations lists the basic qualifications required of DQPs. In brief, persons are eligible to be licensed as DQPs if they are: (1) Accredited veterinarians who are members of AAEP, large animal practitioners with substantial equine experience, or are otherwise knowledgeable in the area of equine lameness as related to soring and soring practices; or (2) farriers, horse trainers, or other individuals knowledgeable about horses whose experience and training qualify them for positions as HIO stewards or judges and who have been formally trained and licensed as DQPs by a certified HIO. Accredited veterinarians who meet the listed criteria do not need to undergo formal training.
In contrast to the current requirements, the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule affirmatively required that veterinarians, as well as all other applicants, complete a formal training program administered by APHIS. In addition, the rule specified continual training of HPIs as APHIS determines to be necessary as a condition of maintaining authorization to inspect horses.
We continue to believe that it is important that all third-party inspectors have substantial equine experience and receive formal training on the HPA before conducting inspections of horses, including veterinarians, who do not typically receive training on the HPA and regulations and their interpretation, the history of soring, the procedures for monitoring horses at HPA-covered events, or the HIO-specific procedures or standards for DQPs within DVM programs. Therefore, we are proposing to revise the basic qualifications of DQP applicants to require that all DQP candidates undergo the formal training requirements set forth in this section. In addition, we are proposing to streamline the qualifications for DQP applicants who are veterinarians. We believe that veterinarians with extensive equine experience are well qualified to be DQPs and that the additional requirements pertaining to AAEP membership and veterinary accreditation are unnecessary and overly restrictive. In addition, these proposed changes are intended to complement the academic and professional experiences of veterinarians by ensuring that all DQPs possess the specialized knowledge and skills needed to conduct inspections under the HPA.

In addition, we are also proposing to make clarifying edits to the second category of persons who may be eligible to be licensed as DQPs. The amended provision would state that, “Individuals who are knowledgeable about equine husbandry or science and whose experience or training would qualify them for positions as stewards or judges for recognized breed associations or equestrian organizations” may be eligible to be licensed as DQPs. The proposed changes to this provision are intended to clarify what kind of knowledge about horses is relevant (husbandry or science) and allow for either experience or training (not necessarily both) as a basis for the basic qualification of DQP applicants. In addition, because the reference to HIOs could be read as circular (insofar as DQP candidates are seeking training and licensure from HIOs), we are clarifying that, by horse industry organizations and associations in this provision, we mean recognized breed associations or equestrian organizations.
