Certification Requirements for DQP Programs
Under § 11.7(b), HIOs desiring a USDA certification to train and license DQPs must submit a formal request for certification and a detailed outline of their program for approval. The outline must include the organizational structure of the HIO and, in brief, must contain:
The criteria to be used in selecting DQP candidates and the minimum qualifications and knowledge regarding horses each candidate must have to be admitted to the program;
A copy of the formal training program, classroom and practical, required to be completed by each DQP candidate before being licensed by the HIO;
A sample of a written examination which must be passed by DQP candidates;
The criteria to be used to determine the qualifications and performance abilities of DQP candidates selected for the training program and the criteria used to indicate successful completion of the training program;
The criteria and schedule for a continuing education program and the criteria and methods of monitoring and evaluating performance for continued licensing of DQPs;
Procedures for monitoring horses in the unloading, preparation, warmup, and barn areas, or other such areas;
The methods to be used to ensure uniform interpretation and enforcement of the HPA and regulations by DQPs and uniform procedures for inspecting horses for compliance with the Act and regulations;
Uniform inspection procedures based on currently accepted methodology and practices in the horse industry for swabbing pasterns and testing the samples for prohibited substances, and for the collection and testing of blood samples for sedatives and other drugs that may cause a horse not to respond to a DQP's examination; and
Standards of conduct for DQPs.
As discussed above, one of the principal concerns that has been identified regarding DQP performance is the need for enhanced training and evaluation. To ensure that DQP candidates are adequately trained and evaluated by experienced equine veterinarians, we are proposing to require that APHIS furnish such instructors for portions of the formal training program. Specifically, we propose that APHIS furnish the instructors who are experienced equine veterinarians for the classroom instruction on the HPA and regulations and their interpretation, the history of soring, the inspection procedures necessary to detect soring, the detection and diagnosis of soring, and related subjects. In addition, APHIS would furnish such instructors for the practical instruction in clinics and seminars using live horses with actual application of the knowledge gained in the classroom. Requests for such instructors and notifications of other courses would have to be made to APHIS in writing at least 60 days in advance of the training.
To ensure candidates demonstrate the knowledge and skills required to be a DQP before obtaining a license, we would require that each candidate pass a practical examination, in addition to a written examination, administered by the HIO and achieve a minimum score of 85 percent on each examination, which demonstrates sufficient mastery of the required knowledge and skills and is the same standard required to become a USEF-licensed steward.
Another principal concern that has been identified regarding DQP performance is the need for sufficient monitoring to ensure DQPs follow inspection procedures and perform inspections consistently, whether APHIS is present or not. To address this concern, we are proposing that HIOs include in their outline for certification the criteria and methods of monitoring and evaluating the performance of DQPs. This outline would need to include methods to ensure each DQP is consistently carrying out his or her duties, including on-site observations by the HIO of the DQP's performance and a description of the procedures the HIO will follow to address situations where a DQP is failing to perform his or her duties in a satisfactory manner and consistently from event-to-event. At no time, however, may an HIO take any action that would interfere with or influence a DQP in carrying out his or her duties or making decisions concerning whether or not any horse is sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations during the DQP's appointed tour of duty.
As discussed above, APHIS has long been concerned about the veracity of inspection under the HPA due to the use of medications and substances that interfere with compliance inspections by concealing signs of soring. Based on recommendations from AAEP and the NAS study, the industry's urging that APHIS include diagnostic methods for evaluating HPA compliance, and the unlawful use of certain medications and substances at HPA-covered events, we are proposing to require that DQPs ensure the collection of pastern swabs and blood samples, in accordance with proposed § 11.21 and the uniform inspection procedures established by their HIOs. HIOs seeking USDA-certified DQP programs would need to include in the outline for their DQP program their uniform inspection procedures based on currently accepted methodology and practices in the horse industry for swabbing pasterns and testing the samples for prohibited substances, and for the collection and testing of blood samples for sedatives and other drugs that may cause a horse not to respond to a DQP's examination. HIOs would need to submit the data and references they relied upon to establish their proposed testing procedures, thresholds, and any sampling methodologies.
As an alternative, we considered specifying which substances are banned, the level at which a substance would cause a violation, and minimum numbers of horses to test. As part of this alternative, we reviewed prohibited substance testing results obtained from horses at HPA-covered events and lists of substances prohibited in horse sports, including the USEF Guidelines & Rules on Drugs and Medications and HISA's list of banned and controlled substances. Although these lists include many of the masking agents we have detected on horses at HPA-covered
(
printed page 73402)
events, they do not include all substances that cause or can reasonably be expected to cause a horse to be sore. In addition, we found that the lists are overbroad, insofar as they include substances that bear no relation to preventing soring. Further, we are aware that the substances used to sore horses have changed over the years, and new substances and new uses for substances continue to be invented. In addition, we anticipate certified HIOs may adopt different testing strategies, including testing a statistically reliable sample of swabs and blood from horses entered in each event or across all affiliated events to which they provide DQP services. To ensure diagnostic testing keeps pace with scientific and technological advances, we believe establishing a performance-based standard, rather than an engineering standard, would be more effective and responsive to emerging trends revealed in testing results. However, we welcome comment on this alternative, including data and information bearing on substances that should be banned or controlled and at what level to prevent soring.
In addition to this proposed action, we considered requiring collection and testing of urine samples for masking agents. However, we elected not to include such procedures in this proposed rule because urine testing often poorly correlates with the actual blood concentration of drugs, making it difficult to determine their impact. However, we welcome comment on this alternative, including data and information regarding its potential use under the HPA.
In addition, we are proposing to add that the uniform procedures established by HIOs must include procedures for the owner, trainer, exhibitor, or other person having custody of or responsibility for any horse allegedly found to be in violation of the Act or regulations by a DQP to contest the DQP's finding. Such procedures could include having a second DQP independently inspect the horse upon request. This proposed change would ensure owners, trainers, and other individuals have an opportunity to appeal both APHIS inspection findings and inspection findings of DQPs, who attend significantly more events than APHIS representatives.
Under the current regulations, HIOs desiring a Department certification to train and license DQPs must submit an outline of their program once for approval. Once approved, an HIO's DQP program is certified indefinitely, unless the program is revoked in accordance with § 11.7(g).
Many HIOs with Department certified DQP programs have been certified for decades. Even though the regulations have been amended and science and technology have advanced in the intervening years, there is currently no mechanism to ensure that the HIO training programs have kept pace with these changes. In addition, APHIS has found it difficult to remove DQP program certifications when an HIO becomes inactive, as there is no process to cancel certifications if the HIO becomes inactive or defunct.
To address these concerns, we are proposing to specify that Department certifications of DQP programs would be valid for 10 years from the date of issuance, unless the certification is revoked in accordance with § 11.7(g) or cancelled due to inactivity. Any HIO wishing to obtain a new DQP program certification from the Department for an additional period of certification may submit a new request in advance of the expiration date of the certification. As an alternative to this action, we considered specifying that DQP program certifications would be valid for 5 years from the date of issuance but determined that a 10-year duration was sufficient to ensure the DQP programs keep pace with changes to the regulations and advances in science and technology. If this provision is adopted, in the final rule we would provide that all existing DQP program certifications and any DQP licenses issued thereunder would expire 1 year after the effective date of the final rule to allow any and all HIOs desiring a Department certification ample time to submit an application for certification and train and license DQPs in accordance with the regulations.
In addition, we would establish a process for cancelling DQP program certifications due to inactivity. Specifically, APHIS will cancel an HIO's certified DQP program if, for at least 5 consecutive years, the HIO has not: Trained or licensed DQPs; had its licensed DQPs appointed by the management to inspect horses; or otherwise met any of the reporting or other requirements. Before cancelling the certification, APHIS will provide the HIO written notification and an opportunity to provide information sufficient to demonstrate maintenance and compliance of its DQP program.
Licensing of DQPs
In addition to requiring that DQP candidates be trained by instructors who are experienced equine veterinarians furnished by APHIS and pass written and practical examinations administered by HIOs with a minimum score of 85 percent on each examination, we are proposing to ensure DQP candidates are evaluated for competency by experienced equine veterinarians, as recommended in the NAS study. Specifically, we would revise the current requirement that prohibits the licensing of any person as a DQP “until such person has attended and worked two recognized or affiliated horse shows, horse exhibitions, horse sales, or horse auctions as an apprentice DQP and has demonstrated the ability, qualifications, knowledge and integrity required to satisfactorily execute the duties and responsibilities of a DQP.” We would revise this requirement by increasing the number of shows that the DQP must attend as an apprentice from two shows to four shows, and require that the DQP demonstrate the ability, qualifications, knowledge and integrity required to satisfactorily execute the duties and responsibilities of a DQP to an APHIS representative at one show after his or her apprenticeship.
Under the current regulations, after DQP candidates complete the formal training program, they participate in continuing education every year thereafter but are not required to complete the formal training program again, even if they are licensed for decades. Similar to the concerns expressed above regarding indefinite DQP program certifications, we believe it is critical that DQPs complete regular training to ensure they stay current on the law and regulations and science and technology, and are regularly evaluated to ensure they can accurately detect and diagnose soring in compliance with the Act. Accordingly, we are proposing to prohibit HIOs from issuing a license to any person as a DQP that is valid for longer than 5 years from the date of issuance. Any licensed DQP wishing to obtain a new license for an additional period of licensure would need to complete all training and licensing requirements for candidate DQPs.
As discussed above, another serious concern that has been raised about DQP performance relates to the need for enhanced screening for conflicts of interest to ensure objective inspection outcomes. As noted in the 2010 OIG audit, DQPs are known to have close ties to the industry and may have conflicts of interest that are not adequately addressed by the current regulations. To address this concern, we propose to strengthen the conflict-of-interest provisions pertaining to DQPs and ensure the integrity of the inspection process. Specifically, we are proposing enhanced minimum standards of conduct for DQPs, which would more closely align with the
(
printed page 73403)
standards of conduct for stewards and judges in other horse sports and include the following:
A DQP shall not exhibit any horse at any horse show or horse exhibition, or sell, auction, or purchase any horse sold at a horse sale or horse auction that includes gaited horse breeds or at which he or she has been appointed to inspect horses.
A DQP shall not have or had within the immediately preceding 5 years any personal, professional, or financial interest in showing, exhibiting, selling, or auctioning TWHs or racking horses, including but not limited to owning, training, riding, or caring for such horses that are shown or exhibited, either for him or herself or for those with whom he or she has immediate family (including a parent, child, spouse, in-laws, and grandparent) or business ties (including as a business partner, employer, or employee).
A DQP shall not inspect horses at any horse show, exhibition, sale or auction that are owned, trained, are being exhibited by, or are being offered for sale by a member of the DQP's immediate family, the DQP's employer, or an officer or board member of the DQP's HIO.
A DQP shall not accept a gift, favor, or employment from anyone (including an owner, trainer, exhibitor, or person having custody of or responsibility for a horse) who has an interest in a horse that is presented for inspection at a horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction containing TWHs or racking horses.
A DQP shall not have an immediate family member, or business partner who works for or is an owner, trainer, exhibitor, or person having custody of or responsibility for a horse who participates in horse shows, exhibitions, sales, or auctions containing TWHs or racking horses.
A DQP shall not participate in the sale, purchase, or ownership of a TWH or racking horse, or supply or provide goods or services related to such horses.
A DQP shall not interact with owners, trainers, exhibitors, or any person having custody of or responsibility for a horse in a manner that creates a potential appearance of a conflict of interest, favoritism, or bias. (Examples of such interactions include, but are not limited to: providing preferential treatment at a show by beginning class inspections early; conducting less thorough, more thorough or different inspections for certain horses (based on trainer or owners); avoiding walking by certain barns while monitoring show grounds; overlooking noncompliance for certain trainers/barns or competitors while enforcing the regulations strictly for others, especially when personal relationships are involved; overlooking noncompliance while attending shows in certain locations and strictly enforcing the regulations in other locations; using non-public information about upcoming HIO rule changes, inspections, or enforcement priorities to benefit trainers, owners, etc.; and putting in a good word to a potential buyer for related to the purchase of a horse in a sale where they quietly receive a commission from the trainer, owner, etc.)
A DQP shall not consume or be under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs while performing official duties.
HIOs would be required to cancel the license of any DQP that violates these standards of conduct. As provided in the current regulations, the DQP may request a hearing before a review committee of not less than three individuals appointed by the HIO within 30 days of cancellation. If the review committee sustains the cancellation of the license, the DQP may appeal the decision of the committee to APHIS within 30 days from the date of their decision, and APHIS will make a final determination in the matter. If APHIS finds, after providing the DQP whose license has been cancelled with a notice and an opportunity for a hearing, that there is sufficient cause for the committee's determination regarding license cancellation, APHIS will issue a decision sustaining such determination. If APHIS does not find that there was sufficient cause to cancel the license, the HIO must reinstate the license.
Requirements To Be Met by DQPs and Licensing Organizations or Associations
Under the current regulations, APHIS requires DQPs to submit records concerning any horse they recommend management disqualify or excuse at a horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction, within 72 hours after the event is over. HIOs must then submit a report to the Department on a monthly basis, based on the information the DQP submitted to them. APHIS is aware the DQPs have encountered postal delays in submitting records to HIOs. In addition, HIOs often submit information on behalf of management, which must be submitted within 5 days of the event. Although HIOs meet their current monthly reporting requirements under § 11.7(d)(3), they routinely encounter challenges with meeting the 5-day deadline required of management, especially regarding the requirement that management must provide copies of each class or sale sheet, as described in § 11.22(a)(6). To better ensure compliance, we are proposing to lengthen the timeframe DQPs have to submit their records to not later than 5 days after the event and the timeframe management has to submit information to 30 days after the event. Concurrently, we would require that HIOs also submit the records they are responsible for providing under § 11.7(d)(3) within the same 30-day timeframe to eliminate any confusion regarding these reporting requirements. As an alternative to this action, we considered setting this deadline to monthly, to match the existing HIO reporting requirements, but determined that 30 days from the date of the event would ensure HIOs adequate time to obtain test results from pastern swabs and blood collection while also allowing for timely monitoring of compliance information and effective enforcement of the HPA.
In addition to lengthening the amount of time DQPs have to submit records to HIOs, we are proposing to expand the information that DQPs must submit to HIOs to ensure HIOs receive information regarding the horses that were swabbed for prohibited substances and from which blood samples were collected in accordance § 11.21, as well as the test results from such inspection. This change would help to ensure HIOs can adequately monitor DQP performance at horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions.

A special Government employee (SGE) as defined in

; and
A Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (or equivalent) who has no fewer than 5 years of direct experience providing veterinary care to horses; and
Free of the conflicts specific to horse protection activities covered under the HPA.

temporary duties for no more than 130 days during a period of 365 days. As SGEs, Appeals Officials would be required to comply with all applicable rules and laws, including financial disclosure and ethics training requirements and conflicts of interest and outside payment, income, and gift prohibitions, and limitations on representational activities.
The time-limited nature of SGE appointments would fit well with the seasonal work of Appeals Officials. The horse show season typically runs from March through November, and events are often held in the evenings and on weekends. To ensure coverage throughout the full season, APHIS would appoint up to four SGEs with staggered schedules over the course of the season. In addition, the standards of conduct and ethics restrictions applicable to SGEs are important for ensuring neutral decisionmakers to hear appeals of APHIS inspection findings at covered events.
Appeals Officials Must Be Veterinarians With No Fewer Than 5 Years of Direct Experience Providing Veterinary Care to Horses
Appeals Officials would be expected to independently review evidence and facts pertaining to APHIS findings of alleged violations of the HPA or regulations, consider the relevance, reliability, and credibility of such evidence and information, and apply the provisions of the Act and the regulations to novel facts and circumstances. This work will require expert knowledge of equine husbandry and science, the HPA and regulations and their interpretation, the history of soring, the inspection procedures necessary to detect soring, the detection and diagnosis of soring, and related subjects. Accordingly, we propose that Appeals Officials be veterinarians with no fewer than 5 years of direct experience providing veterinary care of horses. In addition to this knowledge and experience, Appeals Officials would also be required to complete annual training on the HPA and regulations, and related subjects administered by APHIS prior to serving at any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction.
Appeals Officials Must Be Free of Horse Protection-Specific Conflicts of Interest
In addition to the general conflict of interest restrictions applicable to all SGEs, Appeals Officials would have to be free of conflicts specific to horse protection activities covered under the HPA.
As discussed above, APHIS has long held concerns regarding conflicts of interest by licensed DQPs. The 2010 OIG audit determined that DQPs often failed to inspect horses in accordance with the HPA and disqualify sore horses, likely due to conflicts of interest. The USDA Office of the Judicial Officer and the NAS study reached similar findings, concluding that “DQP examinations are found to be less probative than [USDA] examinations” and that it is “strongly recommended that the use of DQPs for inspections under the current regulations be discontinued.”
In Re: Justin Jenne, Respondent,
74 Agric. Dec. 118, 132, n.16 (U.S.D.A. Apr. 13, 2015) (noting, “[r]outinely, DQP examinations are found to be less probative than United States Department of Agriculture examinations and the Judicial Officer has accorded less credence to DQP examinations than to United States Department of Agriculture examinations.”) (citing Oppenheimer, 54 Agric. 221, 269 (U.S.D.A. 1995) (Decision as to C.M. Oppenheimer); Sparkman (Decision as to Sparkman and McCook), 50 Agric. Dec. 602, 610 (U.S.D.A. 1991); Edwards, 49 Agric. Dec. 188, 200 (U.S.D.A. 1990),
aff'd per curiam,
943 F.2d 1318 (11th Cir. 1991) (unpublished),
cert. denied,
503 U.S. 937 (1992)). In this proposed rule, we are addressing these concerns by proposing additional standards of conduct for DQPs that include enhanced conflict of interest prohibitions, consistent with those applied to stewards and judges in other horse sports.
As with DQPs, we believe it is critical to ensure Appeals Officials are free of conflicts specific to HPA-covered activities to ensure the integrity of the inspection and appeals process. Under this proposal, no person would be able to serve as an Appeals Official that has or had within the preceding 5 years exercised any functions or responsibilities for any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction containing TWHs or racking horses, including but not limited to the management, show manager, DQP, judge, farrier, steward, or HIO for such events. Further, no person could serve as an Appeals Official that has or had within the same period any personal, professional, or financial interest in showing, exhibiting, selling, or auctioning TWHs or racking horses, including but not limited to owning, training, riding, or caring for such horses that are shown or exhibited, either for himself or herself or for those with whom he or she has immediate family or business ties.
Authorization and Training of Horse Protection Inspectors (§ 11.19)
Section 11.19, “Authorization and training of Horse Protection Inspectors,” establishes the application process, qualifications, and training requirements of HPIs and states that APHIS will maintain a list of HPIs on its website. As discussed above, this is the only provision of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule currently in effect. With the proposed withdrawing of the HPI program, this section would no longer be needed.
Responsibilities and Liabilities of Management (§ 11.20)
Under the HPA, it is unlawful to show, exhibit, or enter for the purpose of showing or exhibiting any sore horse in a horse show or exhibition, or to sell, auction, or offer to sell any sore horse in a horse sale or auction. The HPA also prohibits the horse's owner from allowing such activities to occur. In addition, it is also unlawful to show, exhibit, or enter for the purpose of showing or exhibiting, sell, auction, or offer for sale any horse which is wearing or bearing any equipment, device, paraphernalia, or substance that the Department has prohibited by regulation to prevent the soring of horses. The HPA also prohibits anyone from allowing any horse wearing or bearing such items to be shown, exhibited, or sold at a horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction.
The management of each horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction serves as primary enforcer of the HPA. The HPA provides management a choice: (1) Hire a DQP and face liability only if management allows the horse to compete after being notified that it is a sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations; or (2) decline to hire DQPs and accept liability for failing to disqualify a horse that is sore or disallow a horse that is otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations from participating in an event, irrespective of whether such management knows that the horse is a sore.
Among other things, § 11.20 of the current regulations lists the responsibilities and liabilities of management, specifies procedures for management to follow should they be dissatisfied with a DQP's performance, identifies the horses DQPs must physically inspect at horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions and when DQPs must report alleged violations of the Act or regulations to management, and establishes the minimum number of DQPs management must designate and appoint based on
(
printed page 73405)
the number of horses entered in a covered event.
In
Gould,
the court considered a challenge to USDA's “No-Showback Rule,” (
i.e.,
a policy prohibiting horses found sore or otherwise noncompliant with the HPA or regulations from being “shown back” or competing in a subsequent class of the same horse show). The court found that the “No-Showback Rule” likely constitutes an excess of statutory authority because the HPA only requires management to disqualify a horse that is sore or reasonably expects to be sore. The court explained that this “language of the HPA concerns only the present and future existence of soreness—not soreness of the past” and that “allowing for the disqualification of horses that used to be sore flouts the plain text of the HPA.” The court issued an order preliminarily enjoining enforcement of the “No-Showback Rule.”
To align with the court's reasoning in this case, we are proposing to revise § 11.20 to clarify that management must disqualify any horse which is sore from participating or competing in the class in which the horse is entered or shown or the sale or auction in which the horse is being offered for purchase. This change would allow a person having custody of a horse the opportunity to present their horse for inspection after being disqualified by management from a previous class at the same horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction.
APHIS adopted the “No-Showback Rule” at the recommendation of the 2010 OIG audit report that found that exhibitors could use numbing or masking agents on the horse's legs or hooves to prevent the horse from exhibiting pain when being inspected the second time, which could result in the showing, exhibiting, sale, or auction of sore horses. As discussed above, the use of masking agents continues to be a serious concern for APHIS and this proposed rule includes several measures designed to deter and prevent the use of masking agents that interfere with inspection of horses.
In addition, we are proposing technical changes for consistency and to better align this section with the statute. Specifically, we would revise this section to clarify that management must disallow (not disqualify) any horse wearing or bearing any equipment, device, paraphernalia, or substance prohibited under the regulations, while also continuing to make clear that no person shall show or exhibit at a horse show or horse exhibition; sell or auction at a horse sale or auction; allow to be shown, exhibited, or sold at a horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction; enter for the purpose of showing or exhibiting in any horse show or horse exhibition; or offer for sale at a horse sale or auction any horse which is wearing or bearing any prohibited equipment, device, paraphernalia, or substance. As such, management would have the discretion to allow any person having custody of a horse to address certain equipment or other noncompliance that can be adjusted on the spot (such as adjusting a high band), while ensuring that unlawful equipment, devices, paraphernalia, or substances are not used on horses while being shown, exhibited, sold, or auctioned. In addition, we would clarify that management, regardless of whether they appoint and retain a DQP, must remove any horses found to be sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations during actual participation in the show or exhibition from further participation prior to the tyeing of the class or the completion of the exhibition.
Finally, we are removing the requirement that, if event management does not appoint a DQP, they must personally inspect all first-place Tennessee Walking Horses and racking horses to determine whether the horses are sore. Instead, as the Horse Protection Act already requires, event management that chooses not to appoint a DQP will be held responsible if any sore or otherwise noncompliant horse is allowed to compete or participate in the event.
Among other things, paragraph (b)(1) of this section prohibits management from dismissing or otherwise interfering with DQPs during their appointed tour of duty even when management is dissatisfied with their performance. As explained in the 1978 proposed rule, APHIS established this requirement to “protect any DQP from coercion, intimidation, threat, or any other pressure, in order to protect the integrity and credibility of any DQP program.” We have become aware of management contacting DQPs during their tour of duty to discuss inspections of specific horses. Although we believe this activity is clearly prohibited under the current regulations, we are proposing to revise this sentence to expressly state that management shall not contact a DQP regarding his or her inspections during the DQP's tour of duty. Management will continue to have the prerogative of notifying APHIS and the certified HIO that licensed the DQP concerning the reasons management is dissatisfied with the DQP's performance.
Currently, paragraph (b)(2) and (b)(3) contain inspection procedures for DQPs. We propose to consolidate these requirements with the other DQP inspection procedures contained in § 11.21. In addition, we are proposing to revise the requirements currently contained in paragraph (b)(2) which require, among other things, that DQPs observe horses in the warmup ring “whenever possible.” Section 11.7(b)(6) requires HIOs to have procedures for monitoring horses in the warmup area, and § 11.21(b) requires horses to be held in a designated area after inspection that is under observation by the DQP. Because horses are only allowed into the warmup area after DQP inspection, there should be no unlawful devices, equipment, substances or paraphernalia available for use in that area. Nevertheless, while present at shows, APHIS has identified prohibited activities and devices (such as overweight chains) and found syringes and containers with sedatives and other prohibited substances in the warmup area and has been made aware of DQPs removing syringes from the warmup area and of individuals using syringes to inject reversal agents in horses in the warmup area after inspection. Accordingly, we are proposing to require that DQPs inspect any chain carts before allowing them into the warmup area and affirmatively ensure the warmup area and horses in the warmup area are free of unlawful devices, equipment, substances, or paraphernalia after inspection. Examples of such unlawful items include overweight or irregular shaped action devices, syringes, medications, or ointments. If the DQP finds such items in the warmup area, he or she must promptly remove them.
Finally, § 11.20(c) currently requires management that designates and appoints a DQP to inspect horses to use at least two DQPs when more than 150 horses are entered. We are proposing to change this provision to require at least two DQPs when more than 100 horses are entered. This proposed rule enhances the inspection requirements for DQPs, including requiring more thorough inspections and monitoring of the warmup area and ensuring that pastern swabs and blood samples are collected in accordance with § 11.21. We anticipate management of mid-sized shows will need at least two DQPs to perform their inspections in a timely fashion so as not to delay or interrupt actual individual classes or performances in light of these enhanced requirements. Concurrent with this proposed change, we would make conforming edits to the requirement in § 11.21(b) that DQPs shall inspect horses
(
printed page 73406)
no more than 2 classes ahead of time in shows fewer than 150 horses by changing 150 horses to 100 horses.
As an alternative to this proposed change, we also considered setting the threshold at 75 horses entered in the event, and welcome data and information on both options as part of this rulemaking. In particular, we welcome comments on the potential impact of this change on HPA-covered events that involve primarily pleasure horses, which historically have not presented the same level of concern regarding the potential unlawful devices and activities in the warmup area.
Inspection Procedures for DQPs (§ 11.21)
As discussed above, we are proposing changes throughout the regulations to address recommendations to improve the adequacy of the DQP program and strengthen HPA inspections. In § 11.21, we focus our proposed changes on expanding and clarifying DQP inspection procedures to ensure uniform and adequate inspections of all horses examined by DQPs, regardless of whether APHIS is present at the event or not.
Preshow Observation of Horses' Movement
In response to concerns of both the horse industry and animal welfare organizations that the preshow DQP examination procedures were not detailed enough to ensure a uniform and adequate inspection of horses, APHIS amended the regulations in 1990 to expand and clarify the procedures to be followed by DQPs in conducting inspections of horses. These changes included specifying procedures in § 11.21(a) for observation of a horse's movement so the DQP could assess whether the horse moves in a free and easy manner and whether the horse is free of any signs of soreness, such as unusual posture, distressed expression, or a reluctance to move. At that time, APHIS received comments recommending the horse walk in a serpentine or “figure-8” pattern because “indicia of soreness are very likely to appear when a horse is forced to cross over its forelegs when turning.” APHIS agreed with this comment in its October 1990 final rule but stated that the wording of the proposal was sufficient to ensure the DQP required such movement when necessary to help determine if a horse is sore.
However, the NAS study found that current inspection procedures are not sufficiently detailed to allow for sufficient observation of horse movement during preshow inspections because “the distance between the two cones is too short and not all horses complete an entire figure 8. The horse takes three or, rarely, four steps around the right cone and may pivot toward the cone on the left. Furthermore, the horse may not complete a sufficient straight-line walk.” Accordingly, the NAS study recommended that horses should be required to walk around cones in an expanded figure-8 pattern consisting of two adjoining circles, each with a 10-foot radius to allow for better observation of horse movement. The required straight-line evaluation could be done as the horse is walking to the top of the first circle and then back from the figure-8. APHIS agrees with this recommendation of the NAS study and is proposing to amend the regulations accordingly.
Digital Palpation and Examination
Currently, § 11.21 requires DQPs to digitally palpate the front limbs of the horse from knee to hoof, with particular emphasis on the pasterns and fetlocks. The DQP must examine the posterior surface of the pastern by picking up the foot and examining the posterior (flexor) surface. The DQP must apply digital pressure to the pocket (sulcus), including the bulbs of the heel, and continue the palpation to the medial and lateral surfaces of the pastern, being careful to observe for responses to pain in the horse. While continuing to hold onto the pastern, the DQP shall extend the foot and leg of the horse to examine the front (extensor) surfaces, including the coronary band. The DQP may examine the rear limbs of all horses inspected after showing, and may examine the rear limbs of any horse examined preshow or on the showgrounds when he or she deems it necessary, except that the DQP must examine the rear limbs of all horses exhibiting lesions on, or unusual movement of, the rear legs.
As noted in the NAS study, APHIS veterinarians are trained on where to stand and to follow a prescribed pattern of palpation and apply a prescribed amount of pressure using the pad of the thumb. The palpation protocol specifically instructs APHIS veterinarians to use the flat part of their thumb to apply enough pressure to flatten the flesh of the thumb, thus blanching the thumbnail. Referencing a 2008 study on mechanical nociceptive thresholds within the pastern region of TWHs, the NAS study noted that this amount of pressure is well below the threshold to produce a flinch response indicating limb sensitivity in normal TWH limbs.
Haussler, K. K., T. H. Behre, and A. E. Hill. 2008. Mechanical nociceptive thresholds within the pastern region of Tennessee walking horses. Equine Veterinary Journal.
Specifically, the 2008 study evaluated the minimum amount of pressure required to establish reference values within the pastern region of TWHs and found that the amount of pressure needed to flatten the flesh of the thumb or partially blanch the thumbnail is approximately 0.4-0.6 kg/cm
2
, whereas none of the horses studied, which were not sore, responded to pressure less than 6.4 kg/cm
2
using pressure algometry. The study suggested that “a more stringent pressure threshold” could be used to detect soring “with a low risk of false positive tests.” In addition to this study, a 2020 literature review of pressure algometry for the detection of mechanical nociceptive thresholds in horses found that pressure algometry is a reliable and objective method to measure pain responses and found that intra-examiner repeatability is reported to be good but often depends on the level of operator experience using the instrument.
Haussler, K. K. 2020 Review: Pressure Algometry for the Detection of Mechanical Nociceptive Thresholds in Horses. Animals 10, no. 12.
In developing this proposed rule, we considered prescribing the palpation protocol followed by APHIS veterinarians, but this study indicates that the amount of pressure applied under that protocol may be insufficient given the mechanical nociceptive thresholds of the study horses, which had not been sored. We also considered whether to propose the use of pressure algometry as an additional diagnostic tool for assessing compliance with the HPA. However, the 2008 study authors noted that additional study is necessary to establish ranges for padded horses because their shoeing and toe length could result in lower mechanical nociceptive thresholds and to assess the use of the tool in novel environments to determine whether the setting may impact horses' tolerance levels. For these reasons, we believe it would be premature to propose the use of pressure algometry in the inspection of horses under the HPA. However, we welcome additional data and research on this topic.
We are proposing to clarify when a DQP must examine the rear limbs of horses. Currently, the regulations state that a “DQP may examine the rear limbs of all horses inspected after showing, and may examine the rear limbs of any horse examined preshow or on the showgrounds when he or she deems it necessary, except that the DQP shall examine the rear limbs of all horses
(
printed page 73407)
exhibiting lesions on, or unusual movement of, the rear legs.” With the removal of the scar rule, we believe there may be questions regarding what the regulations mean by “lesion” as used in this provision. We are proposing to clarify that DQPs must examine the rear limbs of horses when the horse exhibits abnormal inflammation on or unusual movement of the rear legs. Abnormal inflammation may include redness of skin, edema of the skin, and loss of skin integrity on both hindlimbs in the same approximate degree and in the same approximate area on each leg.
Inspection of Tack
Currently, § 11.21 requires the DQP to instruct the person having custody of a horse to control it by holding the reins approximately 18 inches from the bit shank. Further, the DQP is not required to inspect the horse if a horse is presented in a manner that might cause the horse not to respond to the DQP's examination or if whips, cigarette smoke, or other actions or paraphernalia are used to distract a horse during examination. These provisions were established in the 1990 final rule referenced above and were intended to ensure the integrity and consistency of the inspection process.
Despite these provisions, we continue to be aware of efforts to distract horses during inspection to inhibit their response to pain. In 2011, an owner and operator of a stable that trained TWHs was sentenced for a HPA criminal conviction when a horse trained at the stable was discovered wearing a nerve cord—in this case, a plastic zip tie that distractingly stimulated the horse's gums—in its mouth and found bilaterally sore during inspection. In 2012, the AVMA issued a fact sheet on soring that identified several unethical methods that trainers and owners use to thwart inspections, including the use of a bit burr under the saddle, hand twitch, or surgical staples under the mane just before inspection. In a 2018 open letter to the horse industry, APHIS reiterated the need for DQPs to request the person having custody of the horse to remove tack for inspection when warranted due to these unlawful practices. Most recently, in 2025, a DQP discovered a burr under the saddle of a horse as a means of stewarding the horse during its preshow inspection. To ensure that horses are consistently checked for these and other unlawful devices that may distract them during inspection, APHIS is proposing to require all DQPs to affirmatively inspect under the horse's mane and around and under any tack, including the bit and saddle, for such devices before beginning the physical examination.
Inspection for Prohibited Substances and Masking Agents
As discussed above, APHIS has long been concerned about the veracity of inspection under the HPA because of the use of medications and substances that interfere with compliance inspections by concealing signs of soring. Based on recommendations from AAEP and the NAS study, the fact that there is a common, established practice of blood sampling to test for prohibited medications and medications above therapeutic levels in horse sports around the world, and the unlawful use of such medications and substances at HPA-covered events, we are proposing to amend § 11.2 to expressly prohibit the use of masking agents (such as, but not limited to, sedatives or topical numbing agents) and substances that conceal evidence of soring. In addition to masking soring, such actions may cause a false entry or statement in a report or other required record that DQPs or APHIS representatives prepare and are a grave violation of the Act.
To ensure that horses are consistently inspected for masking agents and substances at HPA-covered events, we are proposing four changes to the DQP inspection procedures. First, we propose to require that DQPs ensure the swabbing of the front pasterns of a percentage of other horses in accordance with the uniform inspection procedures of the DQP's certified organization or association. Second, we propose that, for all horses presented for preshow inspection, DQPs wipe all aspects of the front pastern using a clean cotton pad or cloth and inspect the pad for signs of substances prohibited in § 11.2(c) of the regulations, including dyes, ointments, hair filler, and chemical smells, in accordance with the uniform inspection procedures of the DQP's certified organization or association. Third, we propose that DQPs must ensure the collection of blood samples of any horse that is sore or otherwise not in compliance with the Act or regulations and a percentage of other horses in accordance with the uniform inspection procedures of the DQP's certified organization or association. And fourth, we propose that DQPs ensure the collection of blood samples on TWHs and racking horses tyed first in their class or event.
Consistent with this change, we also would revise the provision in § 11.21(a)(4) for DQPs to decline to examine a horse if it is presented in a manner that might cause the horse not to respond to examination by adding the use of masking agents to the list of actions and paraphernalia that could distract a horse during examination. If the DQP inspects a horse preshow that appears to be or could be sedated, the DQP would be required to inspect the horse after it is shown or exhibited for compliance with the Act and regulations. Moreover, we would make it clear that a DQP may decline to examine a horse if the owner, trainer, exhibitor or other person having custody of or responsibility for a horse takes any other action to interfere or influence the DQP in carrying out his or her duties or making decisions concerning whether or not any horse is sore or otherwise in violation of the Act or regulations.
Inspection of Devices
As discussed above, we are proposing to amend § 11.2(b)(17) to reaffirm the original intent of the prohibition on devices striking the coronet band of the foot of a horse except for soft rubber or soft leather bell boots that are used as protective devices. The intent of this requirement is to prevent the use of devices from being placed on a horse's leg in a manner that will allow such device to strike the coronet band of a horse's foot while such horse is in motion or at rest. Thus, for purposes of HPA compliance inspections, the APHIS representative or DQP will evaluate any chain or action device placed on a horse to ensure it does not land on or strike any location around the circumference of the coronet band. To ensure this evaluation occurs during DQP inspection, we are also proposing to add a conforming change to the inspection procedures in § 11.21. Specifically, we propose that the DQP must verify that any action device or any other device will not strike any portion of the coronet band when the horse is standing or moving during preshow inspection.
Postshow Inspection of Pads
For nearly four decades, the agency has faced challenges with assessing horses shown or exhibited wearing padded shoes for compliance with the HPA. As early as 1979, APHIS observed from its experience in enforcing the Act and regulations that a relationship exists between the use of pads and soring in horses. In its 1979 final rule, APHIS stated that “if the horse industry makes no effort to establish a workable self-regulatory program for the elimination of sore horses, or if such program is established but does not succeed in eliminating the sore horse within a reasonable length of time, the Department will give serious
(
printed page 73408)
consideration to the prohibition of all . . . pads.”
In 1988, after remand from the Court of Appeals, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia recognized that the results of a study conducted by the Auburn University School of Medicine supported a finding that the use of padded shoes resulted in soring and ordered the USDA to institute rulemaking proceedings to promulgate regulations conforming to the requirements of the Act.
Am. Horse Prot. Ass'n, Inc.
v.
Lyng,
681
F.Supp. 949 (D.D.C. 1988).
Among other things, the court stated that the Auburn Study strongly indicated padded shoes “not only can reasonably be expected to cause soreness to a horse, but also can evade detection [of soreness] through the examination techniques employed at horse shows.” In compliance with the court's order, APHIS issued four interim rules and a final rule between 1988 and 1989 that considered various amendments to the list of prohibited devices and equipment, including prohibitions on the use of padded shoes. Ultimately, however, APHIS did not retain certain proposed prohibitions on the use of pads in the 1989 final rule because some pads may be used for corrective purposes. At that time, in response to comments recommending a prohibition on all pads because they can hide objects inserted between the pad and the foot, APHIS also stated that a thorough preshow inspection of a horse combined with the removal of pads to permit visual inspection was an appropriate way of dealing with the insertion of objects, rather than the prohibition of all pads.
More than two decades later, in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, APHIS amended the regulations to prohibit the use of pads and wedges on TWHs and racking horses at horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions, unless the horse has been prescribed and is receiving therapeutic treatment using pads or wedges as approved in writing by a licensed veterinarian. That amendment followed decades of disproportionately high rates of noncompliance found in TWHs and racking horses that compete in padded classes at horse shows and concerns that soring continues to occur through the use of performance packages that can introduce unnatural angulations of the foot or hide signs of pressure shoeing, among other things.
In
Celebration,
the U.S. District Court considered a challenge to the prohibition on all nontherapeutic pads on TWHs and racking horses at horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions. The court found that the prohibition exceeded USDA's statutory authority because pads “do not cause soring and can be used in an appropriate way.” The court vacated the prohibition on nontherapeutic pads in the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule.
While being mindful of the U.S. District Court's order in
Celebration
regarding the HPA's statutory scope of authority, APHIS remains concerned about the disproportionately high rates of noncompliances found in TWHs and racking horses that compete in padded classes at horse shows and the use of performance packages to hide signs of pressure shoeing (including trimming the hoof to expose sensitive tissues and tightly nailing on a shoe or inserting a hard object between the pad and the sole to exert pressure on the sensitive tissue) to cause it to be sore and gain an unfair advantage in competition.
Although DQPs currently have the authority to remove pads as part of their inspection, we are aware that such examinations rarely, if ever, occur. The AAEP, in its 2008 recommendations for the elimination of soring within the TWH industry, recommended the reexamination of selected horses as they exit the ring to include “removal of both front shoes of randomly selected horses” and “visual and hoof tester examination of unshod feet for evidence of methods directed at inducing pain, such as pressure devices and excessive paring of the sole and frog.” Following this recommendation, from 2014 through 2016, the TWHNCA's VAC included shoe removal as a component of its inspection procedures for assessing HPA compliance.
In this proposed rule, we are proposing to require the removal of pads in certain circumstances so that DQPs will consistently inspect for pressure shoeing. Specifically, we would require DQPs to, at minimum, remove the pads on any TWHs and racking horses tyed first in their class or event and any time a DQP deems necessary to assure such horses are in compliance §§ 11.2(b)(13), (b)(18), and (b)(19), except that the DQP may require the removal of any pads on Tennessee Walking and racking horses tyed first in their class or event once per day if such horse tyed first in more than one class or event on a single day. In addition, if a horse tyed first is disqualified following inspection and the class is re-tyed, the DQP would be required to inspect the horse that is subsequently tyed first and require the removal of any pads to assure the horse is in compliance with §§ 11.2(b)(13), (b)(18), and (b)(19). This proposed change aligns with the purpose of the Act (
i.e.,
eliminating soring to promote fair competition) by confirming that top-placed horses are compliant and free of unfair competitive advantages that could be gained through pressure shoeing.
As alternatives to this proposed requirement, we considered having DQPs require the removal of pads on a random basis of a certain percentage of horses during their postshow inspections or all first place horses, including any horse that placed first in two classes on the same day. However, we elected to propose a more flexible standard because of cost, the likelihood of reduced risk of noncompliant alterations occurring between classes, and welfare concerns about repeat pad removal and replacement in the same day. We also considered whether certification requirements for DQP programs should include digital radiography as part of the inspection procedures for DQPs as a means of evaluating horses for prohibited objects and practices that may occur within the pad and shoeing of a horse. We recognize that, although digital radiography is less time-consuming because it generally does not require the removal of the pad, it also has its limitations in that it does not allow the DQP to visually inspect the horse's natural hoof or examine it with hoof testers. In this regard, digital radiography may not detect all causes of pressure shoeing, including trimming the hoof to expose sensitive tissues and certain hard objects that are not visible on radiograph. We welcome comments on these alternatives and the proposed requirements for postshow inspection of pads.
Reporting by Management (§ 11.24)
Under the current regulations, paragraph (a) of § 11.24 requires management to submit information required by § 11.22(a)(1) through (6) within 5 days following the conclusion of any horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction containing TWHs or racking horses for each horse excused or disqualified from being shown, exhibited, sold or auctioned and the reasons for such action. If management does not excuse or disqualify any horse, the management shall submit a report so stating. Similarly, paragraph (b) of this section requires management to inform APHIS within 5 days following the conclusion of any horse show, horse exhibition, or horse sale or auction which does not contain TWHs or racking horses of any case where a horse was excused or disqualified by management or its representatives from being shown, exhibited, sold or auctioned because it was found to be
(
printed page 73409)
sore. This provision has existed in the regulations since 1979.
In situations where management appoints and retains DQPs, APHIS is aware that some HIOs with certified DQP programs that provide licensed DQPs for an HPA-covered event will submit the information required under this section on behalf of management. Although such HIOs meet their current monthly reporting requirements under § 11.7(d)(3), they routinely encounter challenges with meeting the 5-day timeframe established under this part, especially regarding the requirement that management must provide copies of each class or sale sheet, as described in § 11.22(a)(6). Other challenges HIOs have encountered include postal delays in obtaining DQP records and other unforeseen circumstances, such as staff taking personal leave for a death in the family. We believe that lengthening the timeframe for management to submit the information required under this part is warranted and would not adversely affect APHIS' ability to review this information to assess compliance with the Act and regulations. Accordingly, we propose to lengthen the time management has to provide the information required under this section from 5 days to 30 days. Concurrently and as discussed above, we would require that HIOs with certified DQP programs also to submit the records they are responsible for providing under § 11.7(d)(3) within the same 30-day timeframe to eliminate any confusion regarding these reporting requirements.
As an alternative to this action, we considered lengthening this time to monthly, to match the existing HIO reporting requirements, but determined that 30 days would ensure HIOs adequate time to obtain test results from pastern swabs and blood collection while also allowing for timely monitoring of compliance information and ensure effective enforcement of the HPA.

Finally, this proposed rule would require that Appeals Officials appointed by APHIS provide decisions on appeals of APHIS findings to submit information concerning any decisions on appeals to APHIS within 5 days after the horse show, exhibition, sale or auction. This information would include the name and address of the show and the show manager; the exhibitor's number and class number, or the sale or auction tag number of said horse; the name, age, sex, color, and markings of the horse; the date and time of the appeal review; a written response to the appeal and reasons for the decision; and copies of any evidence considered in providing a decision on each appeal. APHIS would require this information to evaluate the effectiveness of its inspection program, monitor the incidences of violations of the Act and regulations, and for use in its enforcement of the Act. APHIS would provide information to the trainer and owner of each horse allegedly found in violation of the Act or its regulations after appeal, including the name and date of the show, exhibition, sale, or auction and the name of the horse and the reason for the finding. Upon request, APHIS would also provide a copy of the Appeals Official's written response to the appeal to any person who had responsibility for the horse at the time of appeal, including the groom, exhibitor, or other person having custody of or responsibility for a horse, in accordance with any applicable laws or regulations, including the Freedom of Information Act (

The Horse Protection Act (HPA, or Act,
44 U.S.C. 1821
et seq.
) prohibits sore horses from participating in horse exhibitions, sales, shows, or auctions covered under the Act. The term “sore” when used to describe a horse includes applying an irritating or blistering agent to the any limb of a horse; inflicting a burn, cut, or laceration on any limb of a horse; injecting a tack, nail, screw, or chemical agent into any limb of a horse; or using any other substance or device on or engage in a practice involving a horse, and as a result of such application, infliction, injection, use, or practice, such horse suffers, or can reasonably be expected to suffer, physical pain or distress, inflammation, or lameness when walking, trotting, or otherwise moving, with limited therapeutic exemptions.
The Secretary of USDA is authorized to issue regulations to carry out the purposes of the Act. The Secretary has delegated such authority to the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS). Within APHIS, the responsibility for administering the Act has been delegated to the Deputy Administrator for Animal Care. Regulations and standards established under the Act are contained in
9 CFR part 11
(referred to below as the regulations), and
9 CFR part 12
lists the rules of practice governing administrative proceedings.
On May 8, 2024, APHIS issued a final rule that significantly revised the HPA regulations (referred to as the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule), which was subsequently challenged in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas and partially vacated on January 21, 2025. We subsequently delayed the effective date of the non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule on three separate occasions.
APHIS is now removing the vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule, and proposing to withdraw the remaining non-vacated provisions. The reasons for the withdrawal are articulated in the preamble of the proposed rule that this economic analysis evaluates. The non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protective final rule include that APHIS would screen, train, and authorize inspectors to conduct inspections at all HPA-covered events; relieve horse industry organizations (HIOs) from regulatory responsibilities; establish new reporting and recordkeeping requirements, including advance notice to APHIS of event details and post-event reporting; and affirmatively require event managers to provide a farrier at events with more than 100 entered horses (or on call for smaller shows), appoint an additional inspector when an event has more than 100 entered horses, and provide HPIs and APHIS representatives with adequate shelter, lighting and access to electricity.
Overall, the non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule introduced modest costs for the industry—including additional costs associated with recordkeeping, familiarization with the new requirements, retaining and appointing an additional inspector when more than 100 horses are entered in a covered event, and costs for equipment like inspection shelters and generators, and a farrier, when needed. In terms of costs to APHIS, the agency estimated that its costs under the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule could increase by up to $3.2 million annually.
The withdrawal of the non-vacated provisions of the 2024 Horse Protection final rule is expected to have negligible economic impact because the rule's major cost-generating provisions—such as establishing a new APHIS-run inspection program, expanding APHIS staff to serve as alternative inspectors, establishing new reporting systems, and implementing nationwide recordkeeping changes—were intended to be funded by APHIS. Additionally, as noted, the 2024 Horse Protection final rule would have imposed modest increase in costs for event managers who already fulfill similar requirements as those contained in the rule. If the proposed rule were adopted, the costs and benefits associated with the non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule would not be realized.
In addition to the withdrawal, APHIS is also proposing several revisions to the current Horse Protection regulations (current regulations) to ensure that the regulations afford due process and better align with the Act. Key proposed updates include:
Addressing longstanding concerns with the adequacy of the Designated Qualified Persons (DQPs) program through enhanced training, evaluation, monitoring and standards of conduct provisions;
Enhancing and modernizing the DQP inspection procedures to better ensure that only compliant horses enter the show ring or otherwise compete or participate in HPA-regulated events;
Strengthening provisions to ensure that exhibitors, management, horse industry organizations and associations (HIOs), and other individuals do not interfere with APHIS or DQP inspections of horses;
Prohibiting the use of masking agents and other substances that conceal evidence of soring (such as sedatives or topical numbing agents);
Removing the scar rule;
Revising APHIS' inspection procedures to require two APHIS veterinarians to independently inspect and concur on a finding of a noncompliance before notifying the individual having responsibility for the horse;
Establishing a process for individuals who are responsible for a horse to immediately appeal APHIS inspection findings to a neutral Appeals Official at the event; and
Clarifying the responsibilities of management for disqualification of sore horses and the prohibitions on horses otherwise not in compliance with the Act or regulations.
The overall objective of the proposed rule is to align the regulations with the HPA and promote more effective and consistent enforcement of the Act and regulations. The principal proposed amendment to the current regulations is designed to address longstanding concerns with the adequacy of the DQP program through enhanced training, evaluation, monitoring, and conflicts of interest provisions. Currently, candidate DQPs must complete 14 hours of training and other requirements before the candidates can obtain a license. Once licensed, DQPs must complete at least 4 hours of continuing education each year thereafter. Under the proposed rule, DQPs would need to obtain a new license every 5 years, which means they would need to complete the 14 hours of training and other requirements every 5 years. Licensed DQPs would still need to complete at least 4 hours of continuing education annually under the proposed rule.
The proposed rule would also reduce burden on HIOs with Department-certified DQP programs by having APHIS furnish experienced equine veterinarians to serve as instructors for 10 hours out of the 14 hours of candidate DQP training and the 4 hours of annual continuing education. For DQP candidate training, the HIO would continue to provide an instructor for 2 hours of classroom on the anatomy and physiology of the limbs of horses, one
(
printed page 73411)
hour of classroom instruction on DQP standards of conduct, and one hour of classroom instruction on recordkeeping and reporting requirements and procedures.
The proposed training changes include provisions that may have offsetting impacts on the total cost for HIOs. Although HIOs will incur lower costs for each individual training session as APHIS assumes responsibility for more instruction hours, the new 5-year licensing program introduces a recurring training cost that does not currently exist. The net economic impact of these changes is uncertain, as it depends on factors such as the average tenure of a DQP, for which we do not have data. It is possible that the increased frequency of training could be largely offset by the reduced cost per session, resulting in a minimal net change to overall training expenditures over time.
HIOs would still be responsible for developing and implementing the DQP training program (aside from the training curriculum APHIS would cover related to the HPA, history of soring, practical instruction, and annual continuing education). We anticipate that these changes will reduce costs for HIOs associated with the provision of instructors and training of DQPs because APHIS would assume responsibility for providing most of the instructors and developing the training for those courses. However, there will be additional costs to HIOs in developing the training program to fit the new requirements, including costs associated with training DQPs to ensure the collection of prohibited substance and blood samples, and monitoring of the warmup area at HPA-covered events. Under the proposed rule, DQPs would have to apprentice at four covered events before being eligible for licensure, whereas the current regulations require apprenticeship at two covered events before being eligible for licensure. HIOs would also be responsible for developing methods to assess DQP performance to ensure consistency across all HPA-covered events affiliated with the HIO, and providing a process that would allow the person having responsibility for or custody of a horse to contest a DQP's inspection finding. Additionally, APHIS would certify HIO DQP programs for a period of 10 years. Currently the programs are certified indefinitely, unless revoked. APHIS invites public comments on the costs to the HIOs and DQPs associated with these changes in the proposed rule.
Given that the proposed rule would involve establishing a new practical examination, DQP performance monitoring, and inspection procedures, it could take HIOs 4-6 weeks to establish compliant procedures and programs. Once they have developed their procedures and programs, it could take HIOs approximately 16 hours to update their outlines accordingly. Developing and implementing the compliant procedures and programs required by this proposed rule could involve some one-time costs for HIOs with DQP programs. The resources and time required to achieve compliance would likely vary across organizations, depending on the degree to which their existing procedures already align with the requirements for a DQP training program under the proposed rule. While it is reasonable to assume some HIOs have robust DQP training programs that are closer to meeting these new requirements, others would likely need to undertake more substantial changes to their programs under the proposed rule. Because neither the number of entities that would need to make significant changes nor the full extent of those changes is known, the overall cost that could be incurred due to this proposed rule is also unknown. We welcome data and information from the public regarding these estimates.
APHIS has historically found that events attended only by DQPs have reported lower rates of noncompliance than events that APHIS attended as well. The proposal includes several provisions designed to ensure consistent DQP inspections whether APHIS is in attendance or not, including enhanced and modernized inspection training and procedures, standards of conduct (including conflict of interest provisions), and procedures for HIOs to monitor DQP performance and follow up on performance problems. Considering the historical trends and contributing factors that are unrelated to the adequacy of DQP performance, it is possible that some DQPs may continue to report lower rates of noncompliance under the provisions of the rule, with costs accruing from missed detections. However, as noted above, APHIS is proposing changes to ensure clear guidelines and processes for conducting inspections, monitoring performance, and addressing DQP performance deficiencies.
With the removal of the scar rule, APHIS anticipates there may be an increase in the number of horses identified as “sore” after showing because the use of otherwise permissible devices (such as action devices) may aggravate preexisting conditions such that, postshow, a horse may exhibit abnormal sensitivity or inflammation on both forelimbs or hindlimbs or otherwise meet the statutory definition of “sore.” In addition, we believe that individuals wishing to gain an unfair competitive advantage may try to conceal signs of soring to pass preshow inspection in subsequent classes by applying masking agents to a horse's pasterns or sedating a horse to alter its response to palpation. However, the proposal includes several measures that will mitigate against these potential adverse outcomes, including prohibitions on masking agents and enhanced preshow and postshow inspection procedures. Overall, we believe these changes would better align the regulations with the statute, provide exhibitors with more opportunities to potentially show or exhibit horses that are not sore, and promote fair competition.
Finally, this rule would strengthen due process protections for participants by providing that APHIS will only notify management of a noncompliance if two APHIS veterinarians independently inspect the horse and concur on the finding. In addition, participants would have the option of immediately appealing the finding to a neutral Appeals Official before disqualification. If the participant did not submit an appeal in time or if the Appeals Official affirms APHIS' finding in whole or in part, APHIS would notify management of its finding. The proposed rule would also clarify the responsibilities of management regarding the disqualification of horses. The proposed rule would make clear that management is required to disqualify a sore horse from the specific class for which it was inspected only, rather than disqualifying the horse from the entire event. The proposal also clarifies that management may permit certain equipment corrections that can be fixed on the spot, thus allowing a horse to be re-inspected for and compete in that same class.
APHIS will incur additional costs associated with the hiring and provision of Appeals Officials at HPA-covered events where APHIS representatives conduct inspections, but we believe the benefits of ensuring due process and better alignment with the Act outweigh these costs to the government. Overall, the benefits of the proposed rule are expected to justify the costs. The proposed changes to the current regulations would promote the humane treatment of horses and fair competition by more effectively ensuring that horses that participate in covered events are consistently inspected and that only horses that are compliant with the HPA and regulatory requirements participate
(
printed page 73412)
in covered events. This benefit is an unquantifiable animal welfare enhancement and would result in greater public confidence that the animals are being treated humanely.
The proposed rule is not expected to adversely impact the communities in which covered events are held because such events are expected to continue. Owners are motivated to show their prized horses and are likely to continue participating in horse shows. Strengthened enforcement of the HPA is expected to also benefit shows, exhibitions, sales, auctions, and participants by improving the reputation of the Tennessee Walking Horse and racking horse industry. Participation in events may increase if the proposed rule were to result in increased confidence by owners in consistent inspections across all HPA-covered events and assurance that individuals who sore horses to gain a competitive advantage are likely to be prevented from participating.
We also estimate that approximately 80 DQPs would require training under the new provisions, which require an increase in DQP services in connection with the proposed requirement that management of covered events with more than 100 horses entered to appoint and retain at least two DQPs compared to the current 150 horses entered. In addition, approximately 12 HIOs would be eligible to submit applications to maintain their DQP program certifications if they were able to meet the enhanced requirements in the proposed rule. The entities affected by this proposed rule are likely small by SBA standards.
APHIS invites public comments on the potential impact of the proposed rule.

Under this proposed rule, proposed § 11.7(b) would require horse industry organizations and associations seeking a new Department certification of their Designated Qualified Persons (DQP) programs to submit additional information on their detailed outline. Specifically, HIOs would be required to add more detail regarding how they will address situations where DQPs fail to perform their duties in a satisfactory manner and the methods used to ensure uniform procedures for inspecting horses for compliance with the Act, including procedures based on currently accepted methodologies and practices in the horse industry for swabbing pasterns and testing samples for prohibited substances and for collecting and testing blood samples for sedatives and other drugs that may mask soring. In addition, HIOs would have to add their procedures for individuals having responsibility for a horse to contest a DQP's finding of a noncompliance in their outline for certification. Certifications would be valid for 10 years under the proposed rule.
In addition, the proposed rule would revise § 11.7(d) to lengthen the time DQPs have to submit copies of information concerning horses inspected at covered events to their licensing HIOs from 72 hours to 5 days and require DQPs to submit new information regarding any horses whose pasterns were swabbed for prohibited substances or from whom blood was collected for testing purposes.
Similarly, this proposed paragraph would also lengthen the time HIOs have to submit information regarding DQP inspections to APHIS from monthly to 30 days following the conclusion of each horse show, exhibition, sale, or auction and make other changes to align the HIO reporting with the DQP reporting requirements concerning prohibited substances and masking agents.
Please note that proposed § 11.24 would lengthen the time management has to submit information to APHIS concerning their horse shows, exhibitions, sales, and auctions from 5 days to 30 days. Accordingly, this proposed change would impose no new burden but would rather allow additional time to fulfill the existing reporting requirements. In addition, the records required for Appeals Officials under proposed § 11.42 pertain to government employees and are thus not subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act.
